text:
Transfer rule: If a phrase uses a bodily location or physical process, then choose the option that preserves a literal biological meaning over idiomatic or metaphorical uses of “digest.”
Error pattern: Success came from disambiguating a polysemous word by anchoring it to the concrete domain signaled by nearby context.
Diagnostic check: Replace the key term with a domain-specific paraphrase; if the full phrase still makes coherent physical sense, keep it, otherwise reject it.
Use when: Relevant for vocabulary-in-context items where one word has both literal physiological and figurative meanings and the sentence includes anatomical cues.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt clearly signals figurative language, wordplay, or discourse about reading, thinking, or communication.

Transfer rule: If choices contrast everyday appearance with scientific composition, then choose the option stating what the thing physically is, not how it looks.
Error pattern: Success came from preferring a mechanism-based definition over vague, figurative, or obviously false descriptions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this describe material nature and cause, or only appearance/feeling?” Eliminate appearance-only answers first.
Use when: Relevant for basic science multiple-choice items about natural objects, where one option gives a real physical explanation and others are superficial.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for perception, symbolism, common speech, or intentionally simplified classroom wording.

Transfer rule: If asked for a trait inherited by every member of a biological group, then choose the defining trait that is universal across the group, not one common in many members.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing diagnostic class-defining features from traits that are frequent, variable, or nonbiological.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Could any legitimate member of the group lack this trait at any life stage?” Eliminate any option that fails universality.
Use when: Apply on classification questions about inherited characteristics shared by all organisms in a named taxonomic group.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about “most,” adult-only traits, exceptions, or acquired/cultural items rather than inherited biology.

Transfer rule: If choices mix living decomposers with a machine/tool, then select the one that cannot perform biological waste breakdown.  
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by ecological role rather than surface familiarity or usefulness.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can it metabolize dead material or recycle nutrients on its own?” Eliminate any nonliving item.  
Use when: Apply this on science questions contrasting organisms, decomposers, recyclers, and man-made devices.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about collecting, transporting, or mechanically processing waste rather than natural elimination.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about change across seasons, then map the date range to the typical temperature trend and pick the effect that follows directly.
Error pattern: Success came from using broad seasonal progression instead of overthinking rare events or secondary consequences.
Diagnostic check: Identify the starting season and ending season, ask “overall colder or warmer?”, then eliminate choices inconsistent with that one-direction trend.
Use when: The prompt compares two calendar points, holidays, or seasons and asks for the most likely environmental change.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question specifies an unusual climate, short-term weather event, or regional exception that overrides normal seasonal patterns.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what becomes visible when looking deeper into a transparent or reflective object, then choose the physically observable internal feature, not metaphorical or impossible outcomes.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering choices by real-world plausibility and literal perception rather than being distracted by fanciful wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option with “Could an observer directly verify this by sight in ordinary conditions?” and reject any that fail.
Use when: Apply this on everyday-knowledge multiple-choice items about vision, materials, and what can literally be seen.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is explicitly figurative, fictional, or asks for symbolic interpretation rather than physical observation.

Transfer rule: If asked what a magnet sticks to, then choose only an item made of ferromagnetic metal, not just any hard or shiny material.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the concept to material properties instead of surface appearance or common usage.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Is it typically iron or steel?” Eliminate wood, plastic, paper, and nonmagnetic metals.
Use when: This applies to object-property questions where everyday items differ mainly by what material they are usually made from.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question states unusual materials, coatings, decorative imitations, or specially magnetized/nonmagnetic alloys.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for seasonal daylight change, then anchor on the solstice/equinox cycle and choose the interval where day length is generally shortest and then begins recovering.
Error pattern: Success came from using Earth-tilt season logic rather than matching isolated month names by familiarity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, place the listed months on a year cycle and verify the span centers on the winter solstice for the relevant hemisphere.
Use when: Apply this to astronomy or seasons questions about daylight duration, Sun angle, or hemisphere-based month ranges.
Boundary: Ignore this when the location/hemisphere is explicitly different, near-equatorial, or the question concerns temperature rather than daylight length.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for reaching a known opposite direction, then choose the tool that identifies the reference direction you can invert.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: used directional-opposites reasoning instead of rejecting all choices for not naming the target direction directly.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Can this option provide a fixed directional reference from which the needed opposite can be inferred?” Eliminate options that are not navigational aids.
Use when: Relevant in orientation, navigation, or analogy items where the needed answer is an indirect means to derive the target.
Boundary: Ignore when the task requires a direct route, movement source, or domain-specific meaning rather than inferring from opposites.

Transfer rule: If choices mix natural replenishing systems with extraction sites or energy devices, then pick the place where finite materials are removed from the ground.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by renewability and by whether the option is a source/extraction location rather than a user of energy.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this location contain and extract limited geologic materials, or does it generate/collect renewable energy?”
Use when: Apply to questions contrasting renewable vs nonrenewable resources, especially where places, structures, and technologies are mixed together.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about resource use, environmental impact, or specific materials rather than the likely location/source category.

Transfer rule: If a device’s operation asks how stored energy reaches the output part, then trace the physical path from source through conductors to the working component.
Error pattern: Success came from using a causal mechanism model instead of matching surface words or irrelevant material properties.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, identify source, transfer medium, and output; verify only one option forms a complete energy-flow chain.
Use when: Apply this to everyday device questions involving batteries, circuits, materials, or how one part enables another part to function.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about biological processes, symbolic definitions, or facts not involving energy transfer through connected components.

Transfer rule: If choices mix standalone predicates with a full tense sequence, then test whether the subject needs a complete predicate describing past, present, and future states.
Error pattern: I matched broad meaning and ignored grammatical fit, especially whether the option forms a natural, fully structured continuation.
Diagnostic check: Read the stem plus each option aloud; reject any choice that is semantically plausible but leaves tense flow, parallelism, or sentence structure incomplete.
Use when: The prompt is an unfinished sentence or clause-completion item with options differing in tense, syntax, or part-of-speech structure.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks only for factual truth, definition matching, or interpretation rather than sentence completion.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about a state of matter’s volume, then compare whether it keeps its own volume or takes the container’s volume.
Error pattern: Success came from linking macroscopic property words to the defining particle-model behavior, not from guessing by wording style.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Would this sample have the same volume after moving it into a larger container without changing amount?” 
Use when: Apply this to basic physical-state questions about fixed vs variable shape or volume under ordinary conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question involves sealed rigid containers, phase changes, or non-ordinary conditions like extreme pressure.

Transfer rule: If choices mix vertebrate classes, then identify the mammal; mammals generally give birth to live young.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each animal by broad biological group before deciding on reproduction mode.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Is it a mammal, reptile, fish, or arthropod?” and verify which group typically bears live young.
Use when: Apply this on basic animal-trait questions where one option belongs to a different major group than the others.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about exceptions or species-level reproductive anomalies within a group.

Transfer rule: If a term names a physical substance or state, then choose the attribute it directly instantiates, not a loosely associated sensation.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the example to its defining property rather than to related temperature words.
Diagnostic check: Replace the example with “presence of water in the air”; if one option matches that definition exactly, prefer it over metaphorical associations.
Use when: Apply this on basic science vocabulary items asking “is an example of what?” where one choice is a direct category/property and others are nearby associations.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are all formal taxonomic classes, require quantitative knowledge, or the example is figurative rather than literal.

Transfer rule: If a question links warm ocean conditions plus abundant moisture to a resulting weather event, then choose the option describing storm formation over unrelated creatures, processes, or locations.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: matching causal environmental ingredients to the meteorological phenomenon they power, not to loosely associated side effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Do the listed ingredients directly fuel a weather system, or do they merely accompany it?”
Use when: Apply this on science items about cause-and-effect in weather, climate, oceans, evaporation, humidity, or storm development.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a byproduct, a location shift, a biological effect, or a purely physical phase-change process.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what happens after reaching a physical threshold, then choose the option matching the standard state change at that threshold.
Error pattern: Success came from applying basic phase-change knowledge and rejecting distractors that describe unrelated or impossible effects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, name the initial state, the threshold, and the expected new state; eliminate any option that violates that transition.
Use when: This fits multiple-choice science items about heating, cooling, melting, freezing, or boiling of common substances.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt changes pressure/composition, asks about exceptions, or involves chemical reactions rather than simple phase changes.

Transfer rule: If a pollutant changes water chemistry toward harmful conditions, then choose the effect that reduces survival or growth of aquatic organisms.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the causal chain from environmental change to biological stress instead of picking a superficially pleasant outcome.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the cause make habitat conditions less suitable, and would that logically lower population, growth, or biodiversity?
Use when: Apply this on ecosystem cause-and-effect questions involving pollution, pH shifts, toxins, nutrient imbalance, or other habitat-quality changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the scenario describes mitigation, adaptation, short-term recovery, or a beneficial input rather than environmental stress.

Transfer rule: If choices mix physical properties with how something looks, then choose the observational/visual property unless the prompt states actual change.
Error pattern: Success came from separating real object attributes from apparent changes caused by viewing or illumination.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would the object itself measurably change, or only how it is perceived from the observer’s position?
Use when: Apply to questions about phases, lighting, perspective, seasons, shadows, or other appearance-versus-reality distinctions.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly describes physical alteration, motion changing distance, or a measured quantity rather than visual observation.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a renewable fuel, then choose the option replenished on human timescales, not one formed over geologic time.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying energy sources by renewal rate rather than by whether they are simply combustible or commonly used.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can this source be regrown or replaced within years to decades?” Eliminate any that require millions of years.
Use when: Apply this to science questions contrasting renewable versus nonrenewable energy or fuel sources.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt asks about efficiency, emissions, current popularity, or whether a material is a fuel at all.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an organism’s goal or function, then choose the option tied to survival or reproduction, not self-harm or waste production.
Error pattern: Success came from using core biology purposes rather than matching superficial wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each choice as promotes survival/reproduction, neutral byproduct, or harmful; prefer the first class.
Use when: Apply this on basic life-science items about what plants, animals, or cells are meant to do.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about byproducts, diseases, failures, or unusual exceptions rather than normal biological roles.

Transfer rule: If a multiple-choice item asks for the nonexistent process in a known scientific cycle, then compare each option to the standard named stages and reject any term not in the canonical list.
Error pattern: Success came from domain-list verification rather than surface familiarity or test-taking tricks.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mentally enumerate the official stages of the cycle from memory and mark whether each option appears exactly as a recognized stage name.
Use when: The question tests membership in a fixed vocabulary set, taxonomy, sequence, or established process.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are synonyms, newly defined terms, or the domain lacks a single standard list.

Transfer rule: If a structure encloses plants with transparent walls/roof, then infer it is used to shield them from damaging cold while allowing light in.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the object’s core function to environmental protection, not to gas control or reducing warmth.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does this option describe protection from harsh cold exposure while still permitting sunlight? Reject choices about gases, cooling, or ordinary conditions.
Use when: Apply this for basic purpose/function questions about gardening, farming structures, or weather-related plant protection.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about chemistry, climate effects, ventilation details, or a non-plant use of the structure.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a planet’s rotation causes, then first match rotation to the day–night cycle before considering secondary effects.
Error pattern: I confused a direct consequence of a motion with a phenomenon influenced by multiple forces and motions.
Diagnostic check: List each choice and ask, “Would this still happen without external gravity or internal geology?” Keep only effects produced by spinning alone.
Use when: Apply this to science items about causes of planetary rotation, revolution, gravity, tides, or geologic activity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about combined causes, dominant influence, or effects of orbital motion rather than axial spin.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a natural cause “produces,” then choose the option that is a direct, immediate effect of that cause.
Error pattern: Success came from separating direct physical effects from unrelated behaviors, long-term formations, or processes needing extra mechanisms.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Would this typically happen immediately from the stated cause alone, without extra agents or steps?”
Use when: Apply this to basic cause-and-effect multiple-choice items about everyday physical phenomena and observable results.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for indirect effects, exceptions, multi-step chains, or domain-specific mechanisms beyond common observation.

Transfer rule: If an object’s common everyday purpose is asked, then choose the option describing its direct, typical function for users.
Error pattern: Success came from matching familiar real-world use rather than overthinking with unrelated medical or body-measurement claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What does an average person use this item for in daily life?” and reject options needing extra sensors or different tools.
Use when: Apply this on basic vocabulary or object-function questions with one ordinary use and several plausible but mismatched alternatives.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item is specialized, multifunctional, or the question asks about uncommon, technical, or context-specific uses.

Transfer rule: If choices mix living things, objects, and environmental factors, then pick the one that directly supports the organism’s biological function.
Error pattern: Success came from linking a plant part to its basic survival need rather than to nearby but irrelevant associations.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option helps this part do its job in growth, energy capture, or survival?” and reject choices without a direct mechanism.
Use when: Apply this on elementary science items about body parts, plant parts, habitats, or needs-and-functions relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about harm, symbolism, human use, or a very specific species-dependent exception.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how a transparent crystal creates rainbow effects, then choose the option describing light passing through the material rather than nearby surroundings or indirect surfaces.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: matched the physical mechanism to the answer instead of picking a vague location or secondary effect.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option state the actual path of light through the object that enables dispersion?” Reject choices that only mention area, room, or reflection target.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items about optics, crystals, prisms, refraction, or rainbow formation from shining light.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about reflected images, ambient lighting, or non-transparent objects.

Transfer rule: If one option is a cave- or darkness-adapted species, then treat loss of light-sensing vision as the leading possibility.  
Error pattern: Success came from using habitat-driven trait inference: extreme environments often cause regression of unused sensory systems.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does any option live permanently without light, and do the others normally rely on vision in open water or surface habitats?  
Use when: Relevant in biology questions asking which organism lacks a common sense, especially when one choice is specialized for subterranean, deep, or lightless environments.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the trait concerns temporary blindness, nonvisual light detection, or when multiple options are equally adapted to darkness.

Transfer rule: If a device’s moving part mainly pushes air without changing its temperature, then choose the effect describing air movement/distribution.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the primary mechanical action from secondary comfort effects people associate with it.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does the device add/remove heat, or just create airflow? If only airflow, prefer the motion/distribution term.
Use when: Relevant for appliance-function questions where an object moves a medium and options mix direct physical action with indirect outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when the mechanism explicitly includes heating, refrigeration, moisture removal, or another process that changes the medium itself.

Transfer rule: If asked for a universal growth requirement, then choose the basic biological necessity over a helpful but optional enhancer or condition.
Error pattern: Success came from separating essential inputs from factors that merely improve growth rate or suitability.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can a healthy plant still grow without this in some cases?” Eliminate anything not strictly required.
Use when: Apply this on life-science multiple choice questions contrasting necessities with beneficial supplements, environmental preferences, or material categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about optimal growth, species-specific needs, or limiting factors in a particular habitat.

Transfer rule: If a resource is replenished naturally on human timescales, then classify it as renewable rather than focusing on usage habits or unrelated material properties.
Error pattern: Success came from using the defining characteristic instead of being distracted by consequences, recommendations, or associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option state what makes the category true by definition, and would it still fit across many examples?”
Use when: Apply this to category-definition multiple-choice items contrasting essential traits with environmental impacts, decay rates, sources, or policy advice.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about best practices, exceptions, rates under specific conditions, or tradeoffs rather than the core definition.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the appropriate unit for a real-world travel distance, then choose the largest common length unit that fits the whole trip.
Error pattern: I matched the scenario to a familiar unit for measuring things in general instead of estimating the scale of the distance.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, estimate the trip in everyday terms; if the value would be in the hundreds or thousands of the smaller unit, switch to a larger practical unit.
Use when: This applies to measurement-word problems involving everyday movement, routes, travel, or distances between places.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about short object sizes, precision measurement, or when a specific scale is explicitly given.

Transfer rule: If a scenario describes connecting a device to power so it can operate, then choose the option about completing the path for electric current.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the everyday action to the underlying physical mechanism rather than surface wording or figurative distractors.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Did the action create a continuous source-to-device-to-return electrical path that enables operation?” If yes, favor the electricity-process choice.
Use when: Apply this on commonsense multiple-choice items about plugging in, switches, batteries, wiring, or devices starting to work after connection.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about cost, motion, invention, symbolism, or outcomes unrelated to electrical flow.

Transfer rule: If comparing ordinary surface activity with a deeper underwater version, then prioritize the physical quantity that increases with depth.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a domain principle instead of matching familiar but less diagnostic words from the prompt.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each option and ask which one changes systematically as depth increases; choose the uniquely depth-dependent one.
Use when: This applies to basic science multiple-choice items contrasting surface vs underwater conditions or shallow vs deep exposure.
Boundary: Ignore this when the comparison is not about depth, or when multiple options are explicitly stated to increase together.

Transfer rule: If several options seem absurd, then choose the one with a real, physically verifiable property of the object rather than rejecting all choices.
Error pattern: I overfocused on eliminating obviously false statements and missed a broadly true factual attribute hidden among distractors.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this be true in ordinary reality?” and “Is it an inherent measurable feature?”; pick the only yes/yes option.
Use when: Relevant for simple knowledge MCQs with joke-like distractors, especially about natural objects, science facts, or physical phenomena.
Boundary: Ignore when the item asks for exceptions, figurative language, or when multiple options could be broadly true without tighter context.

Transfer rule: If choices include tools for imaging faraway celestial objects, then prefer the instrument designed for astronomy over a general distance-magnifying camera accessory.
Error pattern: I matched on a familiar keyword about distant objects and ignored the domain-specific purpose of the device.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option by intended scale and target: tiny nearby, ordinary distant scenes, or astronomical targets; reject anything outside the target domain.
Use when: The question asks which tool is best for viewing or photographing an object extremely far away in space.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about everyday photography constraints, portability, or non-space subjects.

Transfer rule: If choices include near-synonyms and one states the ultimate biological result of the described behavior, then pick the outcome the behavior is designed to secure.
Error pattern: Success came from linking a seasonal preparation action to its long-term purpose, not to a merely immediate activity.
Diagnostic check: Restate the sentence as “This behavior ensures they can ___ during scarcity” and test which option still makes full causal sense.
Use when: Apply for animal-behavior or function questions where an action supports future conditions, seasons, or resource shortages.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for the direct immediate action, definition, or a literal paraphrase of the behavior itself.

Transfer rule: If a noun phrase asks what something “is/are” generally like, then choose the option naming an inherent material/attribute, not a contingent content or condition.
Error pattern: Success came from matching stable category-level properties instead of vivid but incidental associations.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: would this still usually be true across most examples and times? Reject options that depend on location, temporary state, or extra occupants.
Use when: The prompt describes a class of natural objects, places, or things with broad adjectives and asks for a generally true completion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about a specific case, temporary condition, exceptional example, or explicitly variable contents.

Transfer rule: If several choices are specific examples plus one option covering all of them, then verify each example fits the prompt and select the umbrella option.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: grouped category reasoning correctly recognized that subtype choices were all valid members of the same actionable set.
Diagnostic check: List each concrete option, test it against the verb/object requirement, then ask whether any listed subtype fails; if none fail, prefer the inclusive choice.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items with overlapping category and subtype answers, especially everyday object-function questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are mutually exclusive, when wording adds hidden constraints, or when one subtype is only conditionally valid.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks what something is best for “improving” in a local context, then choose the option naming the local environment or conditions affected by that thing.
Error pattern: Success came from matching semantic domain and realistic cause-effect, rejecting choices that were socially, technologically, or temporally unrelated.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, replace each option into the sentence and ask: does it form a natural, plausible statement about what local varieties influence directly?
Use when: Apply this to vocabulary-in-context or common-sense MCQs about agriculture, ecology, or suitability within a place.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item depends on idiom, specialized jargon, or evidence that local items affect non-environmental outcomes.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what electricity does in a conductor, then choose the option describing charge/current moving through a path, not damage, heat return, or literal substances.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping the concept to a basic physical process and rejecting vivid but nonphysical distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option describe motion of electric charge in a material, rather than an effect, metaphor gone too far, or a different phenomenon?”
Use when: Apply this on introductory electricity items about conductors, current, circuits, or simple flow analogies.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about resistance, heating, failure modes, chemical reactions, or safety consequences rather than current motion.

Transfer rule: If a question asks “first and foremost” about a source, then choose the most direct, primary output, not a broader or downstream category.
Error pattern: Success came from separating immediate emission from secondary effects or umbrella descriptions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: is this directly produced at the source, or inferred as a consequence/generalization? Prefer the directly produced one.
Use when: This applies to basic science or everyday-knowledge items contrasting concrete outputs with broader abstractions or effects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly asks for the most inclusive category, mechanism, or ultimate underlying principle.

Transfer rule: If asked what a magnet attracts, then choose the option made of ferromagnetic metal in its usual form, not one that might sometimes contain small metal parts.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a possible component instead of using the item’s standard material and function.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask “Is this commonly steel or iron overall or in its key fastening/working part?” and reject items with merely occasional metal pieces.
Use when: Relevant for everyday-object material questions, especially when some options are composites or can vary by design.
Boundary: Ignore when the question specifies unusual materials, decorative nonmagnetic metals, or a specialized magnetic mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a habitat question asks what supports living things generally, then pick the option naming a basic survival resource, not a preference or entertainment feature.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing biological necessities over descriptive but nonessential traits.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would most organisms struggle without this?” and choose the one tied directly to survival needs.
Use when: The choices mix essential habitat requirements with distractors about popularity, variability, or human-centered extras.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question targets a specific species whose special adaptation makes a usually optional feature decisive.

Transfer rule: If a sky-motion question asks what makes stars shift positions over time, then match the timescale named to the corresponding Earth motion before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from separating two mechanisms instead of grabbing a seasonal distractor based on surface wording.
Diagnostic check: Identify the stated timescale, list candidate motions, and eliminate any cause that cannot produce apparent stellar movement on that schedule.
Use when: Apply this to astronomy items about apparent motion, changing sky positions, visibility patterns, or repeated cycles.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about intrinsic stellar changes, atmospheric effects, or instrument/timekeeping artifacts rather than observer-relative motion.

Transfer rule: If a habitat question asks where an organism can be identified, then choose the broad scientifically valid environment, not a region-specific or overly universal one.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering choices by biological habitat constraints and rejecting distractors that were too narrow or too broad.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option with three filters: required medium, required chemistry, and geographic scope; eliminate any failing one filter.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items about where organisms live, grow, or are found, especially when options vary by environment type versus location.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns a specific species range, migration period, or a named local population rather than general habitat.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about seasons by month and place, then map the month to hemisphere on Earth before choosing.
Error pattern: Confusing opposite hemispheres and not grounding the phrase in the specific planet implied by the context.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which hemisphere has that season during that month on Earth?” then verify the option names a hemisphere of Earth, not a vague region.
Use when: Seasonal timing, months, hemispheres, or planet-reference wording appears in geography or science multiple-choice items.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is fictional, about another planet, or gives local climate exceptions instead of global hemisphere seasons.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the named process of an organism fitting into an environment, then choose the option describing adjustment to conditions, not predation or reproduction.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the biological process asked for to the only term expressing environmental fit.
Diagnostic check: Restate the stem as “What is the process called?” and verify the choice names a process, not an event, relationship, or outcome.
Use when: The item asks for a concept label in ecology or biology and options mix processes with unrelated actions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks what happens to an organism, not the term for a process.

Transfer rule: If asked for another tool-use example, then choose a case where an external object is deliberately manipulated to achieve a goal.
Error pattern: Success came from separating true tool use from body parts, built-in anatomy, or ordinary construction behavior.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Is there a separate object? Is the animal actively wielding it? Would the action fail without that object?”
Use when: Apply this on animal-behavior questions contrasting tool use with instinctive actions, anatomy-based feeding, carrying young, or nest/building materials.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about habitat building, body adaptations, or social behavior rather than object-mediated problem solving.

Transfer rule: If choices mix producers, consumers, and gas exchange, then pick the option describing a source that releases the substance, not one that uses or removes it.
Error pattern: Confused a sink/consumer with a producer/source in a simple ecosystem cause-effect question.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark release, use, remove, or unrelated; only choose one that directly adds the substance to the environment.
Use when: Relevant in basic biology or ecology items about where a substance in air, water, or food chains comes from.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about balance, recycling, long-term storage, or multiple processes rather than a direct source.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the largest or most prominent natural features of a celestial body, then prefer large-scale geological formations over objects or life claims.
Error pattern: Success came from matching broad physical scale and realism, not getting distracted by speculative or tiny items.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare each option by likely surface extent, abundance, and whether it commonly exists there in reality.
Use when: This applies to basic science or commonsense multiple-choice items about planetary surfaces, natural features, and relative size.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is fictional, asks about human-made structures, or defines “biggest” in a special nonphysical way.

Transfer rule: If asked which animals do not compete for food, then compare whether they share habitat and prey; pick the pair with neither overlap.
Error pattern: I matched animals by obvious diet similarity without first checking if they ever feed in the same environment.
Diagnostic check: For each pair, list habitat, typical prey, and feeding zone; if any two items overlap, mark possible competition.
Use when: This applies to ecology or food-competition questions pairing organisms from different environments, body sizes, or diets.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about indirect competition, human-provided food, or species with broad migratory ranges causing overlap.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for evidence Earth changes, then choose a landform or surface feature replacing a living thing, not one living thing replacing another.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by geologic/environmental change versus ordinary biological change or human construction.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this show the ground, water, or rock pattern changed over time? Eliminate anything explained by growth, movement, or building.
Use when: Apply on science items about observable signs of environmental or Earth-surface change across time.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about ecosystems, life cycles, habitats, or human-made changes rather than Earth processes.

Transfer rule: If a question asks who can locate something in darkness, then compare animals by tactile dexterity and night-adapted behavior, not by small size or pet familiarity.
Error pattern: I relied on a superficial association instead of matching the task’s required ability to the animal’s natural traits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the task demands in two words, then eliminate choices lacking both abilities.
Use when: Animal-choice questions hinge on functional traits such as nocturnal activity, manipulation skill, sensing, or foraging behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt depends on wordplay, explicit facts given in the stem, or impossible human-only knowledge.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what precipitation can lead to, then favor landforms made by long-term water erosion or dissolution over tectonic or magmatic features.
Error pattern: Success came from separating direct atmospheric effects from internal Earth processes and matching the cause to the right geologic mechanism.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Can repeated rainfall, seepage, or groundwater realistically create this without plate motion or magma?”
Use when: Apply this on Earth-science multiple choice items linking weather, water, erosion, chemical weathering, and gradual landform formation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt involves tectonics, volcanism, sudden hazards, or asks about indirect climate effects rather than direct geologic formation.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks what someone “thanked” after completing a discovery or invention, then prefer a cause or faculty directly tied to the achievement over a family relation or superstition.
Error pattern: I matched a familiar gratitude target instead of the noun phrase that logically explains the accomplishment.
Diagnostic check: Replace each option in the sentence and ask, “Does this function as the mechanism or basis of the success?” Keep the option with strongest causal fit.
Use when: Relevant for idiomatic completion questions where one choice is personally plausible but another better matches achievement-focused logic.
Boundary: Ignore when the context explicitly mentions family support, luck, dedication, or a ceremonial thank-you outside task performance.

Transfer rule: If choices contrast anatomical adaptations, then match each candidate to the defining function or shape named in the prompt.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying options by biological trait and eliminating nonmembers before comparing likely matches.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: is it in the target group, and does it clearly exhibit the specified feature rather than a different adaptation?
Use when: Relevant in biology multiple-choice items about animal structures, diets, functions, or category membership.
Boundary: Ignore when the question depends on exceptions, metaphorical wording, or requires specialized taxonomy beyond common trait recognition.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what happens to a body resource during increased activity, then evaluate net use and loss before assuming demand means the amount rises.
Error pattern: Confusing increased need for something with an increased level of that thing in the body.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “During higher activity, is this resource being consumed or lost faster than it is automatically replenished?” If yes, favor a decrease.
Use when: Relevant for physiology questions about exercise, metabolism, hydration, energy stores, gases, or heat-related body changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly states external replacement, regulation keeping levels constant, or asks about need/intake rather than current amount.

Transfer rule: If choices ask for the most likely cause of a broad environmental increase, then pick the option that most directly scales the main emitting human activity.
Error pattern: Success came from tracing a simple causal chain and rejecting distractors that are indirect, opposite in effect, or weakly linked.
Diagnostic check: For each option, state “more of this causes more of the measured thing” in one sentence; choose the strongest direct mechanism.
Use when: Apply to basic science or commonsense causation questions with several plausible-looking factors and one dominant driver.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an exception, a specific mechanism, or data-based comparison rather than general likely cause.

Transfer rule: If asked what slows heat transfer, then choose the material that acts as an insulator rather than an energy source or mover.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying options by thermal role: barrier vs things that add energy or increase heat flow.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask, “Does this impede conduction/convection, or does it deliver or spread heat?” Pick only an impediment.
Use when: Apply this on basic heat-transfer questions contrasting insulating materials with sunlight, moving air, radiation, or other transfer mechanisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about speeding transfer, phase change, or when insulation changes because of moisture, thickness, or design details.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks how people escape harmful weather, then choose the option that directly provides shelter or physical protection from exposure.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the core need in the scenario to the option with the most direct functional fit, not broader or indirect ideas.
Diagnostic check: Replace the blank with each option and ask, “Does this immediately keep people out of the weather?” Eliminate choices that are indirect, partial, or unrelated.
Use when: Relevant for common-sense fill-in-the-blank or multiple-choice items about practical responses to environmental conditions or threats.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for a long-term cause, a symbolic meaning, or a group-specific action rather than immediate protection.

Transfer rule: If asked how electrical conductors work, then choose the case where a device is powered by a completed circuit through direct contact with a power source.
Error pattern: I matched any electricity-related action instead of identifying the specific mechanism: conduction through connected conductive materials.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this action explicitly create or maintain conductive contact that lets current flow from source to appliance?
Use when: Relevant for questions contrasting powering by connection versus general appliance use, switching, or safety behaviors around electricity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about insulation, disconnection, switching logic, or hazards rather than how conductors enable current flow.

Transfer rule: If asked for a renewable resource, then prefer something naturally replenished on short timescales and not consumed faster than it returns.
Error pattern: I overfocused on manufactured items that seem eco-friendly instead of checking whether the resource itself is continuously renewed by nature.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does nature replace this directly, repeatedly, and quickly without breeding, mining, or manufacturing?”
Use when: Apply this on science/common-sense questions contrasting natural flows or cycles with products, foods, animals, or extracted materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about durability, recyclability, or responsible product choice rather than strict renewability of the resource.

Transfer rule: If a stem states a deprivation or lack of necessities, then choose the option describing the direct likely consequence, not a remedy, duty, or unrelated requirement.
Error pattern: Success came from matching cause-to-effect and rejecting choices that shift to obligations, production claims, or narrower cases.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this option follow immediately from the stated condition for most living beings without adding a new actor, action, or assumption?”
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items with incomplete stems, broad biological terms, and answers mixing outcomes with prescriptions or specifics.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks for a definition, exception, policy response, or explicitly narrower category.

Transfer rule: If asked what has a metal housing/container, then match each item to its usual packaging material and choose the one commonly sold in cans.
Error pattern: Success came from using everyday object-material associations instead of focusing on the food or drink itself.
Diagnostic check: For each option, say its typical retail container aloud; if only one is commonly metal, select it.
Use when: This applies to questions about an item's housing, container, casing, or packaging material among familiar consumer goods.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt refers to the item’s internal composition, a special product variant, or unusual storage context.

Transfer rule: If options mix broad category words with habitat-specific examples, then choose the term that fits every listed environment.
Error pattern: Success came from using set intersection and preferring the most general valid category over narrower members.
Diagnostic check: For each option, test all named settings one by one; reject any option that clearly fails in even one setting.
Use when: The prompt asks what several different places or groups all have, especially with broad-versus-specific answer choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the best example, a subset, or an exception rather than a universal fit.

Transfer rule: If a moving mass of ice scrapes against rock, then choose the effect caused by abrasion on the rock surface.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the process mechanism to a physical trace rather than picking a temporary or vague condition.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does the option describe a lasting scrape/score mark from friction, or merely contamination, temperature, or appearance?
Use when: Apply this for earth-science questions about contact between moving natural materials and solid surfaces, especially erosion or glacial motion.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about chemical change, short-term conditions, or effects on loose material rather than bedrock.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what medium carries a phenomenon, then match the option that physically propagates through that medium.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by transmission medium rather than by loose association or everyday wording.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: can it travel through air as a wave/disturbance carried by air itself, not merely occur in air?
Use when: Apply this on basic science items about media, carriers, propagation, waves, or how effects move.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns causes, components, measurements, or metaphorical uses of “vehicle” rather than physical transmission.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a universal feature of living things, then choose the process all living things do, not the category they already belong to.
Error pattern: Confused a defining class label with a produced outcome, selecting identity instead of a life function.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is this something life generates or does?” and “Could it merely restate what life is?” Reject restatements.
Use when: Relevant for basic biology items about characteristics shared by all living things, especially with one choice being a broad noun for life itself.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for classification, definition, or examples rather than a feature, function, or result of life.

Transfer rule: If a life-science question asks what food and water are necessary for, then choose the broad function that enables staying alive, not a social setting or descriptive category.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping basic inputs to an organism’s fundamental biological requirement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option describe a universal life process supported directly by nutrients and water for any organism?”
Use when: Apply this on basic biology items about needs, resources, or functions of organisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about environment, relationships, measurement terms, or species-specific behaviors rather than core life maintenance.

Transfer rule: If an item picks up or absorbs a substance, then choose the result describing possession/containment of that substance before a generic state change.
Error pattern: I favored a broad byproduct description over the more direct relation created by the action.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option states what the object now has or holds?” and prefer that over effects like appearance or condition.
Use when: Relevant for everyday action-result questions about absorbing, carrying, collecting, or taking in materials.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt specifically asks for a changed property, sensory quality, or physical condition rather than what is retained.

Transfer rule: If a camouflage question asks why an organism resembles a dangerous species, then first test whether the benefit is predator avoidance via deterrence.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the adaptive function of mimicry rather than picking a general life activity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Who changes behavior after seeing this resemblance—predators, prey, or mates?” Choose the option matching that observer’s response.
Use when: Apply this on biology items about camouflage, mimicry, warning appearance, disguise, or resemblance to harmful organisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the trait is explicitly for courtship, hunting strategy without resemblance, or non-visual behaviors.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about a biological dispersal process, then choose the option naming a natural organism or mechanism that directly performs it.
Error pattern: I favored a human-associated transport idea over a literal biological agent mentioned by the concept.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Can this option physically move the item in nature without metaphor, teaching, or human logistics?”
Use when: The prompt concerns ecology, life cycles, reproduction, dispersal, or other real-world natural processes with mixed literal and figurative choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is explicitly about communication, culture, trade, or symbolic spread rather than physical movement in nature.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why an energy source suits factory power, then choose the option naming a core supply property, not a side benefit or false mechanism.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering distractors by feasibility: reject claims that confuse source with output, add irrelevant fuels, or cite nonessential cleanliness.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option with “Does this directly explain reliable industrial power availability?” and eliminate any that fail that test.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items about energy sources, industrial use, and reasons one source is preferable.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for environmental impact, cost comparison, or a specific technology’s conversion process.

Transfer rule: If choices describe combining substances, then pick the one implying a reaction that creates new substances or changed chemistry, not just contact or dilution.
Error pattern: I overselected a harsh cleaner by association instead of checking whether the prompt’s specific mixture itself evidences chemical change.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: after mixing, is there a plausible reaction product or property change beyond being a physical mixture? Eliminate mere containers plus contents.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items contrasting chemical change with mixtures, dilution, contamination, or simple placement of one material in another.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about physical change, cleaning effectiveness, safety, or when a reaction is explicitly stated elsewhere.

Transfer rule: If asked which option shows day-night from planetary rotation, then choose an actual planet that rotates on its axis and exclude non-planets.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each option by object type before applying the day-night concept.
Diagnostic check: For every option, mark “planet?”, then “has axial rotation?”; eliminate anything failing either test before selecting.
Use when: Relevant for astronomy multiple-choice items mixing planets with moons, dwarf planets, stars, or constellations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about phases, orbital motion, tides, seasons, or non-planetary bodies’ light cycles.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what sustained heat does to a body of water over time, then prefer the direct physical-state outcome before secondary effects on organisms.
Error pattern: I focused on a plausible biological consequence and missed the more primary, system-level result implied by prolonged exposure.
Diagnostic check: List options by causal distance from the stated process; choose the earliest direct effect unless the prompt asks about indirect impacts.
Use when: Apply this to environmental change questions involving long duration, cumulative heating, drying, evaporation, or persistence of a resource.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly targets short-term ecology, species response, or local symptoms rather than the fate of the whole system.

Transfer rule: If a life-cycle question asks what happens after a transitional stage, then choose the option meaning “change into a new form or state.”
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the biological process to a general semantic action, not from surface word association.
Diagnostic check: Restate the stage as “undergoes transformation,” then test each option for whether it denotes adaptation/change rather than size, damage, or gathering.
Use when: Apply this on biology or process questions featuring stages, metamorphosis, development, or before-and-after state changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about a physical action, quantity change, or a specific factual outcome unrelated to transformation semantics.

Transfer rule: If a question asks when something is most effective, then evaluate the device’s core physical function in typical conditions, not the season with the biggest hazards.
Error pattern: I matched to a salient danger context instead of testing where the tool’s mechanism works best.
Diagnostic check: State the tool’s mechanism in one phrase, then compare all choices by asking “In which setting would that mechanism operate most strongly or directly?”
Use when: Seasonal, environmental, or condition-based questions about tools, materials, or natural processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item explicitly asks about safety need, common usage, or exceptional situations rather than peak functional effectiveness.

Transfer rule: If a device’s output is asked in terms of radiant waves, then match that energy form to the appliance’s primary everyday food-preparation effect.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping energy conversion to normal intended use rather than getting distracted by any food item merely heated by the device.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state “input energy, output energy, typical purpose,” and verify the option describes the standard outcome of that appliance.
Use when: The question names a common appliance, asks what electricity becomes or does, and choices mix plausible foods or outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the appliance is specialized, multiple outputs are central, or the prompt asks about a nonstandard use or mechanism detail.

Transfer rule: If an animal-food question asks how survival continues after prey is gone, then choose the stored-energy source before non-nutritive or biologically implausible options.
Error pattern: Success came from applying basic physiology and elimination, recognizing that metabolism can draw on reserves when intake stops.
Diagnostic check: Test each option with “Does this provide usable energy or a known short-term reserve?” and reject anything that does not.
Use when: Apply this to biology or reading questions about starvation, fasting, hibernation, depletion, or survival after feeding stops.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question gives species-specific unusual diets, external aid, or a fictional setting that overrides real metabolism.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where an animal “makes its home,” then choose the option that directly provides nesting/shelter structure, not just a place it may visit.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from familiar examples and picked a broad habitat associated with feeding rather than actual dwelling sites.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could it physically support a nest or regular shelter?” and eliminate choices that are mainly transit, recreation, or resource areas.
Use when: This applies to habitat/home questions, especially when several options are plausible environments but differ in shelter suitability.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about feeding grounds, migration routes, sightings, or species-specific exceptions tied to water or urban living.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a material “will” do generally, then choose the direct physical effect on the device it interacts with before downstream accidents or dramatic outcomes.
Error pattern: I favored an indirect consequence over the immediate mechanism named or implied by the prompt.
Diagnostic check: Identify the object’s nearest affected instrument; ask, “What happens first, physically, every time?” and reject options needing extra conditions.
Use when: The options mix basic material-device interactions with larger situational results in navigation, transport, or tool behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly asks for a rare consequence, a context-specific scenario, or a chain effect.

Transfer rule: If asked for an example of a sense, then choose the option showing direct bodily contact or internal sensory experience.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the term to a first-person sensory modality instead of picking any nearby physical event.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can a person directly perceive this through the named sense without extra inference?” Keep only those that pass.
Use when: Relevant on questions about senses, perception, body awareness, or distinguishing sensation from objects, conditions, or events.
Boundary: Ignore when the term refers to emotion, metaphorical “feeling,” or when multiple senses are intentionally combined.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks what a place “houses,” then match animals by typical habitat before choosing the most dramatic creature.
Error pattern: Chose by salience/plausibility from general wildlife knowledge instead of checking basic place-animal compatibility.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could this commonly live in that setting without special conditions?” Eliminate any that usually belong elsewhere.
Use when: Simple vocabulary or common-knowledge multiple-choice items pair locations, environments, or containers with likely occupants.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt signals fantasy, rarity, metaphor, or explicitly unusual examples rather than ordinary real-world fit.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how an animal reacts under pursuit, then choose the response matching its primary defense in the wild, not a generic fear reaction.
Error pattern: I relied on a stereotyped small-animal behavior instead of comparing species-specific escape or defense strategies.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: Is this behavior the animal’s usual first response to a fast predator—run, hide, leap, or confront?
Use when: This applies to wildlife multiple-choice items pairing animals with likely survival behaviors under threat.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns trained behavior, unusual circumstances, or fictionalized animal traits.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what enables a device to transform ingredients, then choose the option naming the causal physical condition that directly drives the change.
Error pattern: I matched a vaguely related descriptive phrase instead of the mechanism most necessary for the process.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would the transformation still occur without this feature?” and keep the one whose absence would prevent normal operation.
Use when: Relevant for everyday-science multiple choice items about tools, appliances, or environments causing a material change.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about appearance, byproducts, comfort, or a specialized term rather than the operative cause.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what would happen from a loose fastening part, then predict the direct mechanical consequence of reduced attachment.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing the most immediate cause-and-effect outcome, not a repair step or a secondary symptom.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option describe what directly happens when attachment weakens, without adding a fix or an indirect consequence?”
Use when: Apply this to everyday mechanics questions involving loose bolts, screws, fasteners, or parts whose main role is holding something in place.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a remedy, a long-term outcome, or when the part is unrelated to attachment stability.

Transfer rule: If a science term names a major internal part of a planet, then choose the option describing a structural layer, not an extreme position.
Error pattern: Confused category membership with a superlative description; recognized the domain correctly but overstated it.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Is this term one member of a set of planetary layers, or does it mean the absolute innermost/deepest part?” Reject answers using extremes unless the term itself is comparative.
Use when: Relevant for vocabulary questions about Earth science structure, anatomy-like layer systems, or part-versus-position distinctions.
Boundary: Ignore when the term explicitly denotes a boundary, depth ranking, or a specific material rather than a layer category.

Transfer rule: If choices mix ordinary actions with a trait or behavior that helps someone adjust to environmental conditions, then pick the adjustment-focused one.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing adaptive responses from routine activities with no environment-matching function.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Does this specifically reduce a challenge from the surroundings or improve fit to conditions?”
Use when: Apply this on biology, behavior, or health questions asking for adaptation, coping, or adjustment examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about preference, nutrition, entertainment, or any action not tied to environmental demands.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what causes rounded or smooth pebble edges in a river, then choose the active erosive agent that transports and abrades them, not the resulting surface quality.
Error pattern: Confusing an effect or description with the physical process that produces it.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as cause, effect, unrelated agent, or restatement; reject choices that merely name the observed condition.
Use when: The prompt is about landforms, sediments, erosion, weathering, abrasion, transport, or changes caused by flowing water.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks for a property being observed, a biological cause, or a non-erosional setting.

Transfer rule: If a question compares visual ability across very different-sized animals and mentions eye size, then prioritize basic biological scaling: larger eyes generally support better acuity than tiny compound or very small eyes.
Error pattern: I overused nuanced exceptions and species-specific speculation instead of applying the broad comparative principle the question was testing.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rank the compared animals by likely eye size and resolution limit; if one pairing has an extreme size gap, test whether that broad rule alone resolves it.
Use when: Apply this on simple multiple-choice biology items asking for the most plausible cross-species vision comparison from coarse traits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives specialized adaptations, habitat constraints, or non-acuity measures like night vision, field of view, or motion detection.

Transfer rule: If a biology question asks what feature directly enables movement, then choose the specific anatomical adaptation, not a broader shape or effect.
Error pattern: I favored a plausible general trait and ignored the more precise mechanism named by the options.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option names the actual structure that performs the function, rather than a correlated description?”
Use when: Apply this on animal-form/function items with several similar body-feature choices, especially where one is a concrete tissue or part.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a broad outcome, category, or multiple contributing factors rather than one direct mechanism.

Transfer rule: If an analogy is object-to-contained/stored item, then choose the option matching containment, not support, source, or interaction.
Error pattern: I matched a loosely related association instead of identifying the precise structural relation between the pair.
Diagnostic check: State the relation as “X holds/contains Y” or another exact verb, then test every option against that same verb.
Use when: The pair is a noun-noun analogy with several plausible real-world associations between the terms.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the pair is mainly about function, sequence, cause-effect, class membership, or producer-product.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what growth of a body part changes, then choose the option describing the direct functional effect of that part.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping structure to function instead of getting distracted by dramatic or incidental outcomes.
Diagnostic check: Name the part’s main job, then test each option: does it increase that job, merely accompany growth, or contradict normal biology?
Use when: Apply this to basic life-science multiple choice about organs, development, and everyday functions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about disease, injury, abnormal mutation, or species-specific exceptions rather than normal growth.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an additional cause beyond an obvious visible factor, then choose the option naming an underlying physical condition, not a weather event or comparison.
Error pattern: Success came from separating root environmental causes from descriptive but noncausal or secondary phenomena.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, test each option by asking, "Could this generally explain persistence of the state across many places and times, or is it just an occasional accompaniment?"
Use when: Apply this for natural-environment multiple choice items involving climate, surface conditions, or causal wording like "as a result of" and "what other factor."
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a direct definition, a single observed symptom, or a short-term trigger rather than a sustaining cause.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where a physiological process occurs, then identify the organ system responsible for that process before matching any option.
Error pattern: Confusing body regions or unrelated structures with the actual site of the named function.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which organ directly performs this function in basic biology?” then eliminate choices from other systems or structures without that role.
Use when: Relevant for anatomy or physiology multiple-choice items that mix one functional organ with several nearby or familiar but unrelated body parts.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about indirect support, transport pathways, developmental origin, or exceptions rather than the primary functional site.

Transfer rule: If an agent pursues a moving target that changes position, then choose the response that adapts pursuit dynamics rather than abandoning pursuit or resting.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling the practical requirement of continuing the chase, not from surface associations with predator-prey wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option directly help maintain interception after the target’s movement?” Reject options that stop, delay, or ignore the new trajectory.
Use when: Apply this to commonsense action questions about pursuit, reaction, motion, or immediate goal-directed behavior after a change.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about long-term strategy, ethics, biological facts, or when multiple steps beyond the immediate reaction matter.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an essential biological role, then choose the option describing a defining species-wide function rather than a common caregiving behavior.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing necessary role-defining traits from optional, culturally variable, or situational activities.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would this apply as a core function across nearly all cases, or is it merely something some individuals may do?
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items contrasting fundamental biological functions with everyday tasks, preferences, or social roles.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is explicitly about personal habits, social expectations, or non-biological responsibilities.

Transfer rule: If an item describes early plant structures and asks what appears later, then map the organism’s life cycle from bud/flower to fruit/seed before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from using biological progression instead of distractors based on unrelated animals, colors, or quantities.
Diagnostic check: Identify the organism, name the current growth stage, and verify the option matches the next plausible stage or product.
Use when: Apply this on nature questions involving plants, seasons, development, or “wait a while/after some time” wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the change depends on outside agents, hidden constraints, or nonliving processes rather than ordinary growth.

Transfer rule: If a weather effect happens overnight and leaves moisture on exposed surfaces, then choose the consequence involving wet/slippery surfaces, not drying, plant death, or freezing-specific hazards.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the direct physical effect to the most immediate everyday consequence and avoiding answers that require extra conditions.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this phenomenon add liquid water, remove water, or require below-freezing temperatures?” Eliminate any option inconsistent with that state change.
Use when: Relevant for basic science or weather questions linking a common process to a practical surface condition.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt includes temperatures, special materials, or indirect long-term effects that change the immediate outcome.

Transfer rule: If asked for the likely source of an effect, then choose the option that actively produces that effect in ordinary use, not one that merely moves, stores, or lacks it.
Error pattern: Success came from functional elimination based on real-world purpose rather than surface association.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would this typically create the target condition right now?” and eliminate anything inactive, indirect, or unrelated.
Use when: Relevant in everyday-knowledge multiple-choice items about causes, devices, room conditions, or object functions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about unusual setups, hidden mechanisms, or exceptions where a normally indirect object can be the cause.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an example of brighter, clearer reflected light from color, then choose the lighter-colored everyday object over darker or irrelevant items.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the governing property to the option instead of getting distracted by unrelated object traits.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: is the object explicitly light-colored, and does that color plausibly make it easier to see by reflecting more light?
Use when: Apply this on basic science items linking color/lightness with visibility, brightness, or reflection in concrete examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when reflectivity depends mainly on material, finish, or emitted light rather than surface color.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for light splitting into colors by refraction, then choose a transparent faceted object that disperses a beam, not a plain reflective surface.
Error pattern: I overfocused on rejecting mismatches and ignored which option positively demonstrates dispersion in a simple experiment.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does light enter the material, bend, and emerge separated into multiple colors, or does it mostly just reflect?
Use when: Apply this on optics items about rainbow formation, refraction, dispersion, prisms, crystals, droplets, or beam-splitting demonstrations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target phenomenon is only reflection, image formation, absorption, or color from pigments rather than separated white light.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what attracts a pollinator, then prioritize the direct food reward it seeks before secondary cues like smell or other signals.
Error pattern: Chose a noticeable locating cue over the primary biological incentive that drives repeated visitation.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Which option is an actual consumable reward for the animal?” If one is food and others are cues or implausible mechanisms, prefer the food.
Use when: Relevant in basic biology items about plant–pollinator interactions, foraging behavior, or attraction mechanisms.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly asks about navigation cues, long-distance detection, or non-feeding attraction behaviors.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a necessary trait of all living animals, then choose a universal ongoing life process, not an intention, effort, or future need.
Error pattern: Confusing a behavioral tendency or goal-directed act with a basic condition required across all cases.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can a living animal exist right now without this?” Reject any choice that depends on trying, choice, stage of life, or special context.
Use when: Applies to biology items contrasting constant life functions with optional behaviors, reproductive status, or episodic actions.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt specifies a species, developmental stage, unusual environment, or asks about possibility rather than necessity.

Transfer rule: If a phrase asks what an animal must do to find prey “to feast,” then choose the option about predatory behavior, not the mere act of eating.
Error pattern: I matched a surface word from the prompt instead of inferring the necessary characteristic implied by hunting.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the sentence as “needs to find prey because it ___” and verify the choice explains why prey is needed.
Use when: This applies to vocabulary or commonsense questions where one clause implies a role, behavior, or causal property of an animal or agent.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about literal wording, idioms, or when the needed inference is not about predation or causation.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an animal would choose to eat, then compare options to its natural diet category before judging size or realism.
Error pattern: Success came from matching species traits to food type instead of being distracted by whether the prey seems too large.
Diagnostic check: List the animal’s diet class, tag each option as meat/plant/processed/unnatural, and choose the option that best fits the class.
Use when: Apply this on basic biology or common-knowledge multiple choice items about animals, habitats, behaviors, or adaptations.
