Boundary: Ignore this when the species is omnivorous, scavenging, fictional, or the question asks about exceptions, captivity, or unusual cases.

Transfer rule: If a driving-safety question asks why severe weather is dangerous beyond traction loss, then check whether the added hazard is reduced visibility and reaction time.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing common, direct roadway risks over rare, sensational, or indirectly related hazards.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as routine driving effect, improbable event, wildlife distraction, or unrelated disaster; choose the routine effect most directly caused by the weather.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice questions about road conditions, weather hazards, and practical driver safety consequences.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt asks about rare exceptions, vehicle mechanics, or officially listed hazards beyond ordinary driving scenarios.

Transfer rule: If an action reduces waste sent to landfills, then classify its environmental effect as beneficial unless a harmful side effect is stated.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by linking less dumping with reduced pollution and resource strain.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this behavior decrease trash, contamination, or disposal burden without introducing a bigger environmental cost?”
Use when: Environmental-impact questions about reuse, waste prevention, recycling, or keeping materials out of disposal sites.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt includes tradeoffs showing higher emissions, toxicity, or resource use outweigh the waste reduction.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what makes animals leave a habitat, then choose the factor that makes the habitat unable to provide shelter or safety, not merely less crowded or more rewarding.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on survival necessity over attractive but non-forcing conditions.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would this alone push most animals out by removing cover, safety, or livable space?
Use when: Apply on ecology items about migration, dispersal, or habitat change driven by environmental conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about voluntary movement toward improved resources rather than being forced to leave.

Transfer rule: If severe weather adds heavy precipitation while driving, then choose the effect that reduces road visibility and increases hazard.
Error pattern: Success came from applying real-world causal knowledge about weather impairing driving conditions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Would this condition help drivers see farther, or force slower, more cautious driving?”
Use when: Apply to safety/common-sense questions linking weather, environmental conditions, and driving visibility or road risk.
Boundary: Ignore when the question concerns non-driving effects, metaphorical wording, or a stated exception that reverses the usual hazard.

Transfer rule: If a habitat provides all basic survival resources and safety, then predict population health and persistence will improve, not decline or disperse.
Error pattern: Success came from matching complete needs satisfaction to positive biological outcomes rather than reacting to distractors about loss or movement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list needs: air, water, food, shelter, safety; if all are present, verify the choice describes flourishing or stable growth.
Use when: Apply this on ecology or survival questions linking environmental conditions to what happens to an organism or group.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt includes limiting factors, disease, predators, competition, reproduction barriers, or asks about short-term behavior instead of overall survival.

Transfer rule: If asked which item could once have been a flower, then choose the item that can be a matured plant reproductive structure rather than mineral, animal dish, or processed food.
Error pattern: I ignored biological life cycles and matched a static object instead of tracing how plant parts develop over time.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could this physically develop from a pollinated blossom on a plant?” and reject anything requiring unrelated origins or major processing.
Use when: Relevant for everyday-object questions involving origins, growth stages, plant anatomy, or “used to be” transformations.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about symbolism, decoration, artificial shapes, or non-biological resemblance.

Transfer rule: If an item asks how a newborn animal recognizes a caregiver, then prefer innate proximity cues named in the choices over invented sensory mechanisms.
Error pattern: Replaced the question with outside knowledge and chose the “closest” option instead of matching the tested concept.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the prompt using only given wording and ask, “Which option directly fits this mechanism without adding unstated cues?”
Use when: Relevant for early-development, instinct, imprinting, or basic biology questions with simple everyday cue descriptions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly requires real-world accuracy beyond the listed choices or allows multiple mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If a sentence links careless human action to a limited natural supply, then choose the option indicating reduction or depletion.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: matching cause-and-effect in everyday resource logic and rejecting impossible or nonliteral distractors.
Diagnostic check: Replace the blank with each option; keep only one that makes a realistic causal statement about nature and scarcity.
Use when: Apply this to basic commonsense multiple-choice items about environment, resources, consequences, or human impact.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is metaphorical, about renewable recovery under protection, or requires domain facts beyond plain commonsense.

Transfer rule: If a question asks to move an effect without moving its source, then prefer an option that redirects or transmits the effect rather than replacing, stopping, or discarding the source.
Error pattern: Success came from separating the physical object from what it produces and checking which choice changes only the produced effect’s location.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this preserve the original source in place while causing the same output to appear elsewhere?
Use when: Apply to commonsense multiple-choice items involving relocation, indirection, or moving influence, signal, or illumination without moving the originating item.
Boundary: Ignore when the task explicitly requires moving the object itself, creating a substitute, or changing rooms physically.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what may be true after a natural event, then choose the option that is a plausible consequence, not one contradicted by the event.
Error pattern: I matched loosely related ideas instead of checking whether the event would typically cause, prevent, or not affect each outcome.
Diagnostic check: For each option, say “more likely,” “less likely,” or “unrelated” after the event; eliminate any option made less likely by it.
Use when: This applies to commonsense cause-and-effect questions about weather, nature, or everyday events and their likely results.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on specialized facts, metaphorical language, or multiple independent conditions beyond the stated event.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how animals in separate places can share information, then choose the option describing an outward communicative act.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the function required by the prompt with the behavior’s purpose, not just any activity associated with the animal.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this action produce a perceivable signal another individual could receive across distance?” Reject options that are internal, stationary, or noncommunicative.
Use when: Apply this to animal-behavior or common-sense items about interaction, signaling, or exchanging information between separate individuals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns private cognition, rest, posture, or communication without detectable signaling.

Transfer rule: If a hazard question asks what lowers moisture in burnable material, then choose the option describing sustained drying weather rather than irrelevant or wet conditions.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the causal mechanism to the physical effect and rejecting distractors that are absurd, unrelated, or opposite in direction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as dries fuel, wets fuel, irrelevant personnel/equipment detail, or joke; pick only a direct drying cause.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items about environmental causes, fuel conditions, wildfire behavior, or moisture-related risk factors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about suppression tactics, definitions, human roles, or when causation is not the target.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where a physical change happens, then pick the option involving heating or cooling that can change a material’s state.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the science concept to the real-world action instead of choosing an unrelated activity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this action plausibly make a solid become liquid or a liquid become solid under normal conditions?
Use when: Apply this to basic science multiple-choice items about observable state changes in everyday activities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about chemical change, motion, growth, or when no temperature-driven state change is involved.

Transfer rule: If an animal is identified by digestive type, then eliminate options incompatible with that type before considering “common” or “protein” arguments.
Error pattern: Mixed up category knowledge by attributing omnivorous/insect-eating behavior to a strictly plant-eating animal.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this species naturally obtain calories from plants, animals, or both?” Then reject any option outside that category.
Use when: The question asks about a typical diet, natural food, feeding habits, or basic biology of an animal.
Boundary: Ignore this when the species is genuinely omnivorous, the question concerns rare behavior, or the prompt specifies captivity/supplemental feeding.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a usual count over a time unit and options differ wildly, then estimate the real-world baseline first and choose the nearest valid range.
Error pattern: Failed by ignoring domain knowledge and not sanity-checking absurd magnitudes against everyday facts.
Diagnostic check: State the expected value in plain words, compare it to every option, and eliminate any choice orders of magnitude too large.
Use when: Basic factual multiple-choice items about common cycles, frequencies, or quantities with one reasonable range and several extreme distractors.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt uses fictional settings, special definitions, or asks about totals over longer periods rather than a typical interval.

Transfer rule: If a safety question contrasts materials during an electrical storm, then rank conductive metal items as riskier than insulating rubber, plastic, or crystal.
Error pattern: Success came from applying physical properties to hazard assessment instead of focusing on size, fashion, or unrelated wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option by electrical conductivity and whether it sits on the body near exposed skin, then pick the highest combined risk.
Use when: This fits questions about weather, electricity, lightning, shocks, or comparing objects mainly by what they are made of.
Boundary: Ignore this when the threat is not electrical, or when shelter, behavior, grounding, or location dominates material effects.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what likely causes refraction, then choose a transparent material with smooth surfaces where light passes between different media.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the physics definition to object properties instead of picking by familiarity or everyday use.
Diagnostic check: Ask: does light enter and exit this object cleanly, and would its speed change across boundaries enough to bend?
Use when: This fits items about optical effects, especially choices mixing clear solids with opaque, rough, or strongly scattering materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the effect asked is reflection, absorption, diffusion, or when the object is not interacting with transmitted light.

Transfer rule: If a condition is caused by dangerous cold, then choose the option that directly provides safe external warmth.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the medical need to the function of each choice, not surface associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the condition’s immediate treatment goal and eliminate choices that worsen temperature or are irrelevant objects/settings.
Use when: Apply this on everyday safety or health questions asking which nearby item best helps a temperature-related problem.
Boundary: Ignore this when the scenario involves long-term care, hidden risks from heat exposure, or choices requiring specialized medical context.

Transfer rule: If a growth/maturation question asks what tends to happen, then choose the effect that directly follows larger size or added biomass before seasonal or incidental traits.
Error pattern: I overfocused on a familiar association and ignored the core process implied by development over time.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option reflect cumulative growth, a temporary condition, loss, or contradiction?” Prefer the cumulative-growth outcome.
Use when: Relevant for biology items about organisms maturing, increasing in size, or showing long-term developmental change.
Boundary: Ignore when the question targets a special adaptation, seasonal cycle, disease state, or explicitly asks about appearance rather than growth.

Transfer rule: If a sky object shifts position over a few hours from the same place, then first attribute it to Earth’s rotation, not orbital motion or star motion.
Error pattern: Success pattern: matched the timescale to the correct cause instead of choosing a dramatic or too-slow explanation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare the time gap to process scales: hours → daily rotation; months/years → orbit; verify the observer’s location is unchanged.
Use when: The question describes apparent movement of celestial objects across the sky over one night for a stationary observer.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem changes the observer’s location, asks about seasonal changes, or involves long-term stellar motion.

Transfer rule: If a clue specifies material and shape, then map both to the setting most likely to contain discarded man-made objects matching those physical properties.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the choice in object attributes and typical locations rather than surface imagery or scenic associations.
Diagnostic check: List the key noun features, generate one plausible object with those features, then ask which setting most commonly stores or discards such objects.
Use when: A multiple-choice question asks where something would be found based on physical composition, form, or function.
Boundary: Ignore this when options depend on symbolism, historical context, or specialized domain knowledge rather than likely real-world placement.

Transfer rule: If asked which item part comes most directly from rocks, then choose the component made from a mineral/ore, not one only indirectly supported by soil or nature.
Error pattern: I confused indirect dependence on rocks with direct material origin and followed a broad association instead of tracing the actual substance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Was this part physically processed from mined earth material?” and rank directness of source, not environmental dependence.
Use when: Relevant for source-of-material questions comparing plant, animal, synthetic, and mineral-derived parts of a familiar object.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about function, manufacturing step, symbolism, or the item is mainly metaphorical rather than material.

Transfer rule: If a biology item asks what parents pass on when reproducing, then choose a hereditary trait or physical feature, not a behavior, object, or relationship.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying options by inheritance versus non-inherited categories.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each choice with “Can this be encoded in genes and commonly passed from parent to child?”
Use when: Apply this on basic genetics or heredity questions that mix body traits with lifestyle, social, or material distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about learned behavior, cultural transmission, adoption, or environmental effects rather than genetic inheritance.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an optical aid implies about target location, then infer the device’s standard purpose before choosing.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning by using common function knowledge rather than surface wording or synonyms.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What is this tool mainly designed to help with in everyday use?” and verify only one option matches that function.
Use when: The prompt includes a familiar object or tool whose typical use directly constrains the answer.
Boundary: Ignore when the tool is decorative, metaphorical, broken, or the scene gives explicit evidence that overrides typical use.

Transfer rule: If a landform or process term appears, then match the weathering type to a physical agent that breaks rock without changing composition.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by mechanism rather than by surface similarity or unrelated human-made objects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does this option physically abrade, crack, or grind rock, and not mainly alter it chemically or generate energy?
Use when: This applies to earth science questions contrasting weathering agents, erosion processes, glaciers, water, roots, temperature change, or technology distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about chemical weathering, climate impacts, or ecosystem effects instead of rock-breaking mechanism.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what results from Earth’s axial wobble/tilt, then choose the effect tied to climate changes across the year, not map divisions or movement terms.
Error pattern: Confused a physical astronomy cause with an unrelated human-made or geographic category; weak cause-and-effect matching.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the mechanism in five words: “wobble/tilt changes sunlight pattern”; eliminate choices that are administrative, static places, or visitors.
Use when: The prompt links an Earth-motion phenomenon to a recurring global outcome and options mix natural effects with unrelated categories.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the motion described concerns daily rotation, orbital path length, or political/geographic systems.

Transfer rule: If a choice describes a visible atmospheric formation, then prefer it over living creatures when asked about water in the air.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the category requested to the physical state and context, not getting distracted by unrelated concrete objects.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option is a weather/sky phenomenon rather than an animal or solid object?”
Use when: Apply this on basic science items involving states of matter, weather, clouds, steam, fog, or water present in air.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about organisms, symbols, jokes, or when multiple atmospheric options require finer distinctions.

Transfer rule: If flow starts on uneven slopes, then choose the path with the greatest downhill gradient first.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the governing physical variable to the answer instead of distracting surface wording.
Diagnostic check: Compare each option by imagined tilt or height drop over equal distance; pick the one with maximum descent.
Use when: Apply this to terrain, drainage, rolling, sliding, or any motion primarily driven by gravity across differently sloped paths.
Boundary: Ignore when another force dominates, surfaces differ strongly in permeability/friction, or the question concerns long-term spread rather than initial movement.

Transfer rule: If choices mix food/water resources with a strong decay or predator cue, then choose the option signaling danger avoidance over attraction.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing animal risk cues over tempting habitat or forage features.
Diagnostic check: For each option, mark attract, neutral, or avoid based on typical herbivore behavior; pick the strongest avoid cue.
Use when: Relevant for wildlife-behavior questions asking what an animal would avoid, approach, or tolerate among environmental features.
Boundary: Ignore when the species is a scavenger/carnivore, is habituated to carrion, or the question depends on unusual local conditioning.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what something has “in endless supply” while growing, then prefer the basic medium/resource inherently around it over abstract conditions or unrelated products.
Error pattern: Success came from eliminating impossible categories and selecting the mundane environmental support item, even when wording felt awkward.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: is this a physical, routinely present growth medium/resource for the subject during expansion, rather than a byproduct, ingredient, or absence-state?
Use when: Apply this to common-sense multiple-choice items about organisms, growth contexts, and everyday environmental associations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt targets a specialized biological mechanism, figurative wording, or a clearly technical definition.

Transfer rule: If a biology item asks about “changes in structure/form,” then identify the life-cycle transformation process, not a separate ability or habitat trait.
Error pattern: I matched a familiar amphibian fact instead of the concept named in the prompt, confusing metamorphic change with function.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the stem in one phrase; then reject choices that describe regeneration, loss, or breathing unless they explicitly show developmental body-form change.
Use when: This applies to life-science questions about development, stages, metamorphosis, or how an organism’s body changes over time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets a specific adaptation, behavior, physiology, or repair ability rather than developmental transformation.

Transfer rule: If your explanation identifies a concept, then map it back to the option by rereading every choice and selecting the paraphrase that matches that concept.
Error pattern: Correct underlying reasoning, but failed at answer selection by misaligning the explained idea with the labeled option.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, restate your reason in 3–6 words and verify one option expresses the same idea; if labels differ, fix the selection.
Use when: Multiple-choice items have silly wording, paraphrases, or joke-like distractors that can obscure which option matches your reasoning.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not option-mapping, such as open-response questions or cases where two choices are truly equivalent.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is necessary to make a common device function, then choose the option that supplies its basic operating input or power source.
Error pattern: Success came from matching real-world mechanism knowledge to the device instead of being distracted by thematic or humorous associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask “What directly enables this object to work?” and verify the choice is physically required, not merely related in mood, context, or imagery.
Use when: Apply this on everyday-object questions where one option is a functional requirement and others are entertainment, metaphorical, or environment-based distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about symbolism, wordplay, fictional settings, or nonliteral interpretation rather than actual operation.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what would help plants multiply, then prefer organisms that directly enable pollination or seed formation over those that mainly eat plants or compete with them.
Error pattern: Success came from linking the biological process needed for reproduction to the organism’s ecological role, rather than choosing by familiarity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as pollinator, herbivore, pest, or unrelated, and select only one with a direct reproductive benefit.
Use when: Apply this on garden, crop, ecology, or life-science items asking which addition increases plant reproduction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about survival in harsh habitats, vegetative cloning, soil chemistry, or nonliving interventions.

Transfer rule: If a needed resource becomes scarcer while demand stays similar, then predict competition or conflict will increase.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a cause-and-effect ecology rule instead of matching surface wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: did the resource amount decrease, and would fewer units force more organisms to seek the same limited supply?
Use when: This fits questions about populations, shared resources, scarcity, competition, conflict, or carrying-capacity style relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt states demand also falls, resources are not shared, or a special mechanism reverses scarcity effects.

Transfer rule: If asked which event causes human-driven environmental change, then select the option requiring deliberate human action, not a natural process.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating agent-caused events from recurring natural disturbances that happen without direct human involvement.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: “Would this still occur without people?” Eliminate any option answered yes.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items contrasting human impacts with weather, hydrology, fire, ecology, or other natural events.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about indirect human influence on natural processes or when multiple causes can interact.

Transfer rule: If a stem asks about axial tilt and seasons, then choose the option describing opposite seasonal timing or seasonal events across regions, not unrelated geography or biology.
Error pattern: I matched a broad topic word and ignored whether the completion formed a coherent seasonal relationship.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, paraphrase the sentence with each candidate and ask, “Does this describe a real consequence of opposite seasons caused by tilt?”
Use when: The prompt concerns Earth’s tilt, hemispheres, seasons, calendars, or simultaneous conditions in different places.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about daily rotation, moon phases, migration, plant growth specifics, or nonseasonal landforms.

Transfer rule: If asked how liquid on the ground gets into the air, then choose the process where liquid changes into vapor.  
Error pattern: Success came from matching the question’s direction of movement and state change, not just picking any weather-related process.  
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this option move water upward by turning it into gas, rather than bringing it down or keeping it solid?”  
Use when: Relevant for water-cycle or phase-change questions involving movement from surface to atmosphere.  
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about water falling from clouds, staying frozen, or moving underground or across land.

Transfer rule: If a concept is a phase-change point, then choose the option that directly shows the resulting state or transition, not a generic example of the original state.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the scientific definition to a concrete observable state change rather than relying on everyday association.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it visibly indicate the material has crossed the threshold into the target state?
Use when: Apply this to science questions linking temperature points, state changes, and real-world representations or examples.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a numerical value, a process cause, or a symbolic definition rather than a depiction.

Transfer rule: If asked to identify an environmental change, then choose the option showing a change in nonliving conditions or seasonal physical surroundings, not just an animal’s behavior or use of habitat.
Error pattern: I confused an organism’s action within an environment with a change to the environment itself.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “What in the surroundings is different before vs. after?” If only the organism’s activity changes, eliminate it.
Use when: Relevant in science items contrasting organism behaviors, habitat use, and observable environmental or seasonal changes.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks about adaptation, feeding, movement, or habitat selection rather than environmental change.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what use will decrease as an alternative grows, then choose the directly displaced counterpart, not a same-direction or unrelated category.
Error pattern: I matched on surface wording and positive association instead of identifying the inverse replacement relationship.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, fill the template “more of X means less of Y because Y is the substitute being replaced”; reject choices that increase with X or are unrelated.
Use when: Relevant for trend, substitution, tradeoff, or cause-effect multiple-choice items about rising use of one thing reducing another.
Boundary: Ignore when the stem asks about coexistence, complements, independent effects, or broad environmental consequences rather than direct displacement.

Transfer rule: If a biology question asks what all members of a body structure category share, then choose the universal anatomical property, not a function, joke choice, or unrelated medical term.
Error pattern: Success came from screening for a trait that applies to every instance rather than overweighing vivid distractors.
Diagnostic check: For each option, test “Would this still be true for every normal example of the structure?”; eliminate any choice failing universality or relevance.
Use when: Relevant for anatomy or physiology multiple-choice items asking about all, always, every, or general characteristics.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about exceptions, specific subtypes, pathology, or comparative differences rather than a universal trait.

Transfer rule: If an item asks what receives “artificial sun” from a device, then choose the living thing that directly needs light for growth.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the device’s function to the biological need, not to unrelated animals or objects.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option commonly requires light exposure to support photosynthesis or cultivation indoors?” and eliminate the rest.
Use when: Apply this to everyday-tool vocabulary questions where a product’s purpose must be linked to the correct target organism or use case.
Boundary: Ignore this when the device is for heat, decoration, or habitat support rather than supplying growth-oriented light.

Transfer rule: If asked which material can form an optical shape, then prefer a substance that can be molded and is at least translucent over opaque solids or living things.
Error pattern: I overfit to speculative treatment of an unlikely material and ignored basic physical suitability.
Diagnostic check: For each option, test three filters: nonliving, shapeable into flat faces, and able to transmit light; eliminate any failing one.
Use when: The choices are materials or objects and the task depends on physical properties like transparency, rigidity, or moldability.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about symbolism, biology, or named uses rather than direct material properties.

Transfer rule: If asked which thing eats other creatures, then choose the option that is a predator/carnivore rather than a plant-eater or nonliving thing.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each option by feeding role in the food chain before selecting.
Diagnostic check: For every choice, mark it as nonliving, herbivore, omnivore, or predator; pick only one that regularly hunts or consumes animals.
Use when: Apply on basic biology or commonsense multiple-choice items contrasting animals, diets, and living versus nonliving categories.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about unusual cases, symbolic meanings, or species with flexible diets not captured by simple labels.

Transfer rule: If a question asks where jumping is hardest, then compare surface gravity/weight there and pick the location with the greatest downward pull.  
Error pattern: I relied on intuitive familiarity and irrelevant surface-type concerns instead of the governing variable for jump difficulty.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rank all choices by approximate gravitational acceleration or “how much heavier you’d be” and ensure the chosen answer matches the maximum.  
Use when: This applies to multiple-choice questions about ease or difficulty of physical actions across planets, moons, or other celestial bodies.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends mainly on atmosphere, terrain, equipment, or asks about survivability rather than raw jump effort.

Transfer rule: If a question sounds biological but the choices are absurd settings, then test for wordplay or a pun before using subject-matter knowledge.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a language-based riddle rather than forcing a literal science interpretation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Can the key term combine with any option into a familiar phrase, joke, or sound-based meaning?”; if yes, prioritize that match.
Use when: The prompt is short, whimsical, and paired with implausible answer choices that make factual reasoning unlikely.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when options are realistic, the wording is technical, and one answer can be verified directly by domain knowledge.

Transfer rule: If choices mix habitat-specific animals with one that commonly lives on land or in freshwater, then choose the one not restricted to the ocean.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each option by typical habitat instead of being distracted by all being animals.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask “Can this species normally be found away from saltwater oceans?” and eliminate any that are exclusively marine.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice questions asking for the item that does not belong by environment, biome, or habitat.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about rare exceptions, life stages, or temporary movement outside usual habitat.

Transfer rule: If choices mix body features with preferences or personality, then choose the directly observable anatomical trait as the inherited one.
Error pattern: Success came from separating genetically passed physical characteristics from learned, cultural, or preference-based attributes.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could this be seen on the body at birth or tied to structure?” and eliminate items needing experience or upbringing.
Use when: This applies to basic inheritance questions contrasting physical traits with tastes, habits, emotions, or social behaviors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about complex behavioral genetics, prenatal effects, or traits explicitly defined as nonphysical.

Transfer rule: If a list asks for items with a material-science property, then test each choice against the defining class first.
Error pattern: Success came from category filtering—separating true members of a technical material class from superficially similar objects.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Is this a metal or metal-derived material studied by that field?”; exclude any biological or nonmetal item.
Use when: Relevant in exclusion, odd-one-out, or classification questions involving domain-specific categories of materials.
Boundary: Ignore when the field explicitly includes composites, biomaterials, or metaphorical uses rather than strict material-class membership.

Transfer rule: If a prompt asks what may occur when an object is used, then test common physical actions directly involved in operating it before abstract or metaphorical effects.
Error pattern: Chose a figurative or broad association instead of the concrete motion most tightly linked to the item's use.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Could this literally happen as part of normal operation?” Prefer the one requiring no extra context or uncommon interpretation.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice vocabulary or commonsense questions about typical actions, effects, or sounds tied to using a tool or object.
Boundary: Ignore when the question clearly targets idioms, symbolism, side effects, or domain-specific exceptions rather than ordinary operation.

Transfer rule: If choices contrast mixed liquids with merely assorted objects, then prefer the option where substances are physically combined into one material.
Error pattern: Mistook a collection of separate items for a scientific mixture; overfocused on separability instead of actual combining.
Diagnostic check: Ask: after combining, do the components occupy the same sample uniformly enough that one scoop contains both, rather than remaining countable pieces?
Use when: Relevant for basic chemistry classification questions distinguishing mixtures from sets, organisms, or age/category groupings.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is about heterogeneous collections explicitly treated as mixtures, or when multiple answers are allowed.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how a stationary organism appears in a new location, then choose the mechanism involving movement of its reproductive propagules by external agents.
Error pattern: Success came from rejecting anthropomorphic or magical explanations and matching the phenomenon to normal life-cycle transport.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list whether the organism itself can locomote; if not, look for dispersal of seeds, spores, eggs, or similar structures.
Use when: Apply this on basic biology items about spread, colonization, range expansion, or appearance in a new habitat.
Boundary: Ignore this when the organism is actually mobile, or when the question is about evolution, growth from hidden parts, or human transplantation.

Transfer rule: If asked what a living thing needs to move, then choose the option that supplies biological energy or sustenance, not a surrounding material.
Error pattern: Success came from linking movement in organisms to internal resource requirements rather than unrelated objects or environmental substances.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each choice with “Would lack of this directly prevent a living body from generating motion because it cannot fuel itself?”
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice questions about living organisms, basic needs, survival functions, or causes of movement.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns nonliving motion, habitat description, tools, or metaphorical movement.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an animal uses speed to catch, then choose a typical prey item from its natural diet, not predators or plants.
Error pattern: Success came from matching predator-prey relationships and filtering out biologically implausible targets.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: is it edible for this animal, commonly hunted, and realistically captured using the stated ability?
Use when: Apply this to animal-behavior multiple choice items involving diet, hunting, locomotion, or ecological roles.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is figurative, about human use, or depends on a special context overriding normal diet.

Transfer rule: If a trait converts sunlight into usable power, then choose the subject with the strongest, most reliable direct light exposure and practical energy demand.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning matched the function to environmental conditions instead of being distracted by familiar organisms or irrelevant setting details.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare options on two axes—sunlight availability and usefulness of harvested energy—and pick the highest combined fit.
Use when: Apply this to adaptation or technology-benefit questions involving energy capture, environmental resources, or choosing who gains most from a function.
Boundary: Ignore this when the key difference is not resource availability or when the trait’s main benefit is unrelated to power generation.

Transfer rule: If choices mix living and nonliving things, then pick the one that must take in nutrients to grow and maintain life.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by biological life status rather than surface familiarity or human-made usefulness.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it eat or absorb nutrients, grow through metabolism, and carry out life processes on its own?
Use when: Apply this on basic science questions contrasting organisms with materials, objects, or substances.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns artificial systems needing energy, plant exceptions requiring special wording, or non-growth-related properties.

Transfer rule: If a condition implies active burning, destructive reaction, or physical harm, then choose the option indicating damage or deterioration.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a hazardous process to its likely negative state instead of being distracted by neutral or positive wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this process usually preserve, improve, or harm the object in ordinary cases?” Eliminate choices inconsistent with harm.
Use when: Apply this for commonsense multiple-choice items about cause-and-effect, especially physical processes, safety, or condition changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt signals irony, metaphor, unusual exceptions, or a specialized context where the process is controlled and non-damaging.

Transfer rule: If a mirror question asks what happens as you move closer or farther, then judge the apparent image size from changing viewing distance, not physical change.
Error pattern: Ignored perspective/optics and answered from literal physical reality instead of the perceived visual effect the question targeted.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Is the prompt about appearance in a mirror?” If yes, compare angular size at two distances; closer means larger-looking.
Use when: Applies to questions about mirrors, images, apparent size, motion toward/away, or what an observer sees rather than what physically changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the setup specifies actual body change, nonvisual effects, distorted mirrors, or asks about absolute physical size.

Transfer rule: If two like conductive pieces are joined end to end, then infer the conducting path becomes longer and remains continuous unless a failure mechanism is stated.
Error pattern: Success came from applying basic circuit continuity and rejecting dramatic physical changes not implied by the setup.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the prompt describe simple contact only, or does it add heat, force, damage, or a power source that would change the material?
Use when: This fits questions about ordinary physical consequences of joining conductors, wires, or path segments in a basic electricity context.
Boundary: Ignore this when the scenario includes insulation, loose contact, corrosion, extreme current, cutting, or any condition that prevents continuity or changes the material.

Transfer rule: If a question compares effects at different elevations, then choose the outcome consistent with water moving downhill and collecting in lower areas.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a basic physical principle instead of getting distracted by absolute wording or implausible exceptions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Where would runoff or rising water accumulate first—higher ground or lower ground?”
Use when: This fits terrain, drainage, flooding, gravity, runoff, or any item contrasting low versus high locations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the scenario adds barriers, pumps, sealed drainage, or other mechanisms that override normal downhill water flow.

Transfer rule: If options mix tangible items with mental states or abstract concepts, then choose the physically measurable object.  
Error pattern: Success came from classifying choices by whether a common instrument can directly interact with them.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: can I place it on the device and obtain a reading without interpretation or inference?  
Use when: The question asks what a tool can measure and the choices vary between concrete objects and intangible concepts.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the instrument is specialized to assess inferred properties, signals, or self-reported states rather than direct physical objects.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what can calculate or measure distance, then choose a physical measuring tool rather than a sensation, object with unrelated use, or mental act.
Error pattern: Mistook a nearby associated idea for the item whose primary function matches the task.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask, “Is this specifically designed to quantify length?” and reject anything that cannot produce a standardized distance reading.
Use when: Relevant for everyday-function multiple-choice items about tools, measurement, or object-purpose matching.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is metaphorical, asks about estimation without tools, or allows nonstandard informal methods.

Transfer rule: If a scene shows a large round impact-like cavity, then favor a high-energy external strike over ordinary animal, weather, or gradual-force causes.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the physical shape and scale to the only mechanism capable of producing that kind of sudden crater.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each option’s implied process and ask: can it plausibly create a wide, bowl-shaped hole quickly and directly?
Use when: Apply this to commonsense science questions about landforms, damage patterns, or cause-and-effect explanations with several everyday distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when evidence points to excavation, erosion over time, or when the prompt asks about symbolism, fiction, or nonphysical causes.

Transfer rule: If options mix habitat-appropriate natural materials with a living thing from a different environment, then choose the environmental mismatch.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each option by typical setting instead of overthinking geology details.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could this normally exist or occur in that location without special circumstances?” and eliminate mismatches.
Use when: Relevant in common-knowledge multiple-choice questions about places, ecosystems, materials, or organisms found in a setting.
Boundary: Ignore when the question specifies unusual exceptions, human transport, fossils, metaphorical usage, or fictional worlds.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what something “may be,” then choose an example that can produce or constitute it, not an energy source, liquid category, or unrelated material.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying options by relationship type and selecting a plausible feedstock/example rather than a byproduct or non-fuel source.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can this reasonably be used to make the target category?” Eliminate items that are only inputs like light, broad substances, or impossible examples.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items testing category membership, examples, sources, or materials used to make something.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for definitions, exclusive requirements, or metaphorical/fictional uses rather than real-world examples.

Transfer rule: If a choice contrasts a specific material with a broad category, then prefer the category when the action describes restoring living or natural assets.
Error pattern: Overcommitting to a vivid concrete image instead of matching the abstraction level implied by the wording.
Diagnostic check: Classify each option by type—material, state, substance, or general resource—and pick the one that fits “restore/replace” in an ecological sense.
Use when: The prompt involves gardens, habitats, trees, wildlife, conservation, or other natural systems and asks what is being replaced.
Boundary: Ignore this when the context clearly names a prior physical surface or structure being removed or rebuilt.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what someone avoiding a nutrient would stop eating, then choose the option commonly made from or rich in that nutrient, not items with negligible traces.
Error pattern: Overweighted tiny natural amounts and ignored the typical dietary association between a food category and the targeted nutrient.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Is this food primarily composed of, or commonly identified with, the nutrient being avoided?” and eliminate trace-only cases.
Use when: Relevant for nutrition, ingredient, or category questions that rely on common food composition rather than strict biochemical exceptions.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt specifies added vs natural sources, processing details, medical diets, or unusual formulations.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what increases when individuals are born, then choose the quantity counting members, not resources, systems, or side effects.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the event to a direct consequence at the species level rather than a loosely associated concept.
Diagnostic check: Rephrase as “more births means more ___ of that group”; accept only an option that is literally a count of members.
Use when: Apply this on basic cause-and-effect multiple-choice items about population changes, group size, or direct outcomes of life events.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about indirect impacts, limiting factors, long-term trends, or broader ecological consequences.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what changes a physical environment, then choose the option that can directly perform the stated physical action in ordinary life.
Error pattern: Success came from grounding the choice in real-world causal capability instead of abstract, emotional, or implausible associations.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this entity literally create the described physical effect by itself?” and eliminate any that cannot.
Use when: Apply this to commonsense multiple-choice items about animals, objects, or agents causing concrete environmental changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is metaphorical, fictional, or defines unusual powers or symbolic meanings.

Transfer rule: If a sentence describes a trait change that helps survival in conditions, then choose the option meaning adjustment to environment, not movement, death, or offspring.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the example to the broad biological process rather than a related life event.
Diagnostic check: Replace the blank with each choice and ask: does it describe a survival response caused by conditions?
Use when: Apply this to fill-in-the-blank biology items about organisms responding to climate, habitat, predators, or resources.
Boundary: Ignore this when the sentence asks for a one-time action, location change, population outcome, or reproductive process.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what makes a device stop functioning, then choose the option that directly changes its control or power state.
Error pattern: Success came from separating causal controls from irrelevant descriptive attributes.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Would changing only this immediately start or stop the device without altering unrelated surroundings?”
Use when: Apply this on common-sense multiple-choice items about everyday objects, actions, and cause-effect relations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on technical exceptions, hidden mechanisms, or metaphorical wording rather than direct physical control.

Transfer rule: If asked which process forms a natural deposit or accumulation, then choose the environmental process that physically creates or carries material.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the effect to a real-world causal process rather than being distracted by unrelated actions or impossible choices.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can this directly produce or transport particles in nature?” Eliminate any option that cannot.
Use when: Apply this on basic science vocabulary questions about causes, formation processes, weathering, erosion, deposition, or natural material buildup.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is figurative, about human-made systems, or depends on a specialized definition outside ordinary physical processes.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which item is integral to many plants’ survival, then choose the one with a direct ecological function in plant reproduction.  
Error pattern: Success came from using functional biology, not familiarity or association with common animals.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does this organism regularly transfer pollen or otherwise directly enable seed/fruit production across many plant species?”  
Use when: Relevant for life-science MCQs about ecosystem roles, mutualism, pollination, or species that support plant life cycles.  
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt targets a specific plant, nonreproductive survival factor, or an indirect food-web effect rather than a broad cross-species role.

Transfer rule: If a question names an organism as a decomposer, then choose the option describing food from dead or decaying nonliving organic matter.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a biology role term directly to its definition instead of being distracted by absurd choices.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the term’s definition in plain words and verify one option matches that definition exactly.
Use when: Apply this on life-science multiple choice items that test ecosystem roles, feeding relationships, or vocabulary-function matching.
Boundary: Ignore this when the organism is identified as a producer, consumer, parasite, or when the question asks about habitat rather than food source.

Transfer rule: If a term describes a physical geologic process, then choose the landform or material change directly produced by that process, not a climate state or human-made thing.
Error pattern: Success came from matching process type to its immediate natural result and rejecting unrelated category distractors.
Diagnostic check: Classify each option as natural landform, environmental condition, or artificial object; keep only options in the same causal category as the process.
Use when: Apply this on Earth science multiple-choice items asking what erosion, weathering, deposition, or tectonic action creates over time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about indirect effects, definitions, timescales, or intentionally figurative wording.

Transfer rule: If a choice makes a literal physical effect from a machine sound quirky but plausible, then test basic mechanism before preferring a vague catchall.
Error pattern: I overused a generic “common phrase” distractor instead of checking which option had a real-world causal link.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can the thing directly cause this in ordinary reality?” and eliminate anything metaphorical, category-mismatched, or impossible.
Use when: Short multiple-choice items use humor, wordplay, or odd pairings and one option may describe an actual side effect or interaction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is purely idiom recognition, metaphor interpretation, or asks for the most figurative expression.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a plant “eats,” then choose the source of nutrition plants make or obtain biologically, not what an animal consumer ingests from them.
Error pattern: I projected the eater’s food form onto the eaten organism instead of identifying the organism’s own nutrition mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each organism as producer or consumer and ask, “Does it make its own food, absorb nutrients, or hunt prey?”
Use when: Apply this on ecology or food-source questions involving plants, animals, or who gets energy from whom.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about unusual exceptions explicitly described, like parasitic, carnivorous, or experimentally altered plants.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which body feature enables a specific sense, then match the organ specialized for detecting that stimulus.
Error pattern: Success came from linking function to anatomy instead of being distracted by unrelated but noticeable traits.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask, “Does this part directly receive or amplify the relevant signal?” Reject parts that mainly aid movement, covering, or another sense.
Use when: Apply this on animal adaptation or form-function multiple-choice items about sensing, feeding, moving, or protection.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about behavior, habitat, or when several parts contribute and the task asks for a broader mechanism.

Transfer rule: If asked which everyday item is most like a planet in component makeup, then compare bulk material type and choose the geologic, mineral-based object.
Error pattern: Success came from matching dominant composition category rather than surface appearance, use, or presence of a single shared substance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label its main material as mineral/rock, liquid, processed food, or mixed container contents; pick the one mostly made of natural solid minerals.
Use when: Apply this to analogy questions about what object most closely matches Earth-like composition, structure, or basic material class.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about size, shape, life support, atmosphere, or a specific layer instead of overall composition.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a part is like after switching on a glowing device, then map the effect to the nearest everyday temperature descriptor among the choices.
Error pattern: Successful pattern—used causal knowledge about electrical heating and selected the closest colloquial synonym rather than demanding a perfect technical term.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the physical effect, list likely synonyms, and verify one option matches that effect better than all others.
Use when: Apply this on simple science-vocabulary MCQs where activation causes heating, light, or another familiar physical change.
Boundary: Ignore this when options depend on technical definitions, trick wording, or evidence that the item’s state does not follow the usual causal process.

Transfer rule: If a sentence asks what enables an animal to endure hunger, then choose the option naming a physiological energy reserve, not a mental state or activity.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the causal mechanism in the subject matter rather than being distracted by human-like traits.
Diagnostic check: Replace each option in the sentence and ask, “Does this directly supply stored energy or reduce energy need in real biology?”
Use when: Apply this on natural-world, animal-survival, or common-knowledge causation questions with one concrete bodily factor among abstract distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is figurative, psychological, or about behavior, motivation, or social causes rather than physical survival mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If asked what makes something electrically insulated, then focus on the outer surface material that contacts the environment, not the hidden interior.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from a familiar insulating material and ignored which part determines electrical isolation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What surface would a hand or wire touch, and is that surface nonconductive?” If yes, insulation is plausible.
Use when: This applies to questions about insulation, shielding, coatings, casings, or objects made of multiple materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about total conductivity, internal current paths, grounding, or thermal insulation instead of electrical contact safety.

Transfer rule: If choices mix tangible physical objects with abstract ideas, then prefer the option that can be directly affected by the stated physical process.
Error pattern: Success came from filtering by real-world causality instead of picking metaphorical or impossible targets.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Can this event physically alter or damage it in ordinary life?” and eliminate any answer requiring figurative meaning.
Use when: Relevant for everyday commonsense multiple-choice items about effects, properties, or interactions of things.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly signals metaphor, poetry, symbolism, or fictional rules beyond normal physics.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what all living organisms are fundamentally composed of, then choose the biology term for the substance of living cells, not everyday materials.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a basic life-science definition instead of being distracted by familiar but nonbiological words.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option name a universal living-cell substance taught in basic biology, or just a common material or plant-specific fluid?”
Use when: Apply this to elementary biology items about defining traits, composition, or basic structure of living things.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about habitat, nutrition, plant transport, or nonliving mixtures rather than organismal composition.

Transfer rule: If a question links storm-driven moving liquid to its effect, then choose the broad damage outcome rather than unrelated creatures, geology, or a narrow process.
Error pattern: Success came from matching cause-and-effect semantics and rejecting options from the wrong domain or scale.
Diagnostic check: List each option’s category; keep only effects plausibly produced by storm water, then prefer the most general direct consequence.
Use when: The prompt describes natural forces in motion and asks what they cause, especially with mixed plausible and implausible categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a specific mechanism, scientific term, or non-storm context requiring technical precision.

Transfer rule: If asked which feature must be present for a process, then pick the option naming an essential internal structural condition, not incidental surface phenomena.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing causal necessities from vivid but irrelevant or merely associated features.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Could the process still occur without this?”; eliminate anything answerable “yes” or not part of the system’s mechanism.
Use when: This applies to science multiple-choice items about required conditions, mechanisms, or system parts versus environmental details.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are all mechanism-level, the question asks for examples/effects, or domain knowledge shows no listed condition is actually necessary.

Transfer rule: If an animal/object is damaged, then choose the function directly supported by that structure, not an unrelated ability.
Error pattern: I matched a dramatic action to a salient but impossible ability instead of checking biological realism and mechanism.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What does this body part or object actually do, and which option depends on that role?”
Use when: Apply this to commonsense multiple-choice items about damage, tools, body parts, habitats, or cause-and-effect functions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is metaphorical, fictional, or explicitly describes nonreal abilities or symbolic meanings.

Transfer rule: If a safety question asks what can be used to observe a bright natural event, then prefer an indirect viewing method over direct optical devices or ordinary wearables.
Error pattern: I overfocused on technically possible equipment and ignored the safest commonly intended method in basic public-safety questions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option as direct view, indirect projection, or normal protection; reject direct view unless a required safety accessory is explicitly included.
Use when: The choices involve eye safety, light intensity, household items, and a single best method for general users.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly supplies certified protective gear or asks about expert setups with stated safeguards.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a resource from a site “can be related to,” then infer its origin or source process, not nearby equipment or extraction machinery.
Error pattern: Mistaking associated tools or infrastructure for the underlying substance or causal origin being asked about.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, restate the noun asked for and ask: “Is my choice the produced resource/source category, or just something used to obtain it?”
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items about natural resources, energy origins, extraction sites, or “comes from/related to” wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly asks for a device, mechanism, platform component, or operational technology.

Transfer rule: If choices mix materials and fuels, then classify each by whether its source replenishes on human timescales.  
Error pattern: Success came from applying source-based resource classification instead of surface familiarity or product category.  
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Does nature replace its raw source quickly enough for repeated harvest without geologic formation?”  
Use when: The question asks about renewability, sustainability, or renewable vs nonrenewable resources among everyday materials.  
Boundary: Ignore this when “renew” means repair, recycle, refill, or legally extend something rather than ecological resource replacement.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to detect a physical property, then choose the action that directly exposes that property to an observable test.
Error pattern: Successful reasoning comes from matching the target property with a simple measurement, not picking a loosely related bodily action.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would doing this produce visible or tangible evidence of the property within seconds?
Use when: Apply this to everyday-science multiple choice items about identifying moisture, temperature, force, odor, or other observable properties.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about causes, definitions, or long-term effects rather than immediate detection.

Transfer rule: If all options seem bad, then choose the one with a plausible moisture-bearing biological source over inert or impossible actions.
Error pattern: I rejected every choice instead of ranking them by real-world mechanism and relative feasibility.
Diagnostic check: Ask: which option could physically contain extractable liquid or water-rich tissue, and which options cannot add fluid at all?
Use when: Relevant for survival, hydration, nutrition, or first-aid questions with several absurd distractors and one minimally viable natural source.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about safety, legality, symbolism, or when biological material is known harmful without hydration benefit.

Transfer rule: If options mix real physical sources with living, fictional, or impossible entities, then choose the option that plausibly contains the material in nature.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: classify each option by real-world existence and whether it can physically contain or host the target substance.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Is this real, and would this substance normally occur there?”; eliminate any option failing either test.
Use when: Apply on basic science or common-knowledge multiple choice asking where a material, element, or object is found.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is metaphorical, fictional-world based, or asks about dietary/trace presence in organisms rather than natural occurrence.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a pet animal is likely fed, then choose the option matching its natural diet and realistic captive feeding practice.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping species class to typical prey rather than being distracted by edible-but-implausible or nonfood options.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would a normal owner commonly give this, and does the animal naturally eat it whole and safely?
Use when: Apply this to everyday-animal multiple choice items about likely food, care, habitat, or behavior using common knowledge.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt specifies unusual training, emergency feeding, fictional animals, or a specialized husbandry exception.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the natural source or producer of an item, then choose the option naming the living category that generates it, not materials, drawings, or places.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the item to its biological producer instead of matching superficial word associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Can this option actually grow or make the item in nature?” Eliminate any option that is nonliving, representational, or merely a location.
Use when: Apply this to basic source-origin questions with mixed choices including organisms, objects, depictions, or habitats.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about storage, use, composition, or a symbolic/figurative source rather than real-world production.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what is lacking while a phenomenon is occurring, then identify the condition required for that phenomenon and choose the thing whose absence would prevent it.
Error pattern: I inverted the logic, selecting the needed medium instead of the missing condition incompatible with the observed event.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “Observed event happens → required conditions present; therefore what is lacking must be something that would stop it.”
Use when: Apply this to commonsense science items about necessary conditions, exclusions, or “cannot happen if absent” relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks what is present, most abundant, or merely associated rather than logically incompatible.

Transfer rule: If a living thing is moved between environments, then compare basic survival needs to the new setting and choose the effect that improves access to a needed resource.
Error pattern: Success came from need-based elimination: reject choices that contradict well-known requirements or confuse absence of one resource with gain of another.
Diagnostic check: List the organism’s essentials—light, air, water, nutrients—then mark whether the new environment increases, decreases, or blocks each one before selecting.
Use when: Apply this to simple science items about habitat changes, growth conditions, or movement from poor conditions to natural outdoor settings.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on a special species trait, hidden context, or a non-biological meaning of the words.

Transfer rule: If a term names a physical medium in basic science, then choose the option describing what it carries or transmits, not unrelated everyday uses.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: mapping a domain-specific noun to its core function rather than to familiar but irrelevant associations.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What moves through this thing in standard textbook definitions?” Eliminate choices that are social, biological, or environmental mismatches.
Use when: The question asks for the role of a scientific object, material, or system in elementary physics or general science vocabulary.
Boundary: Ignore this when the term is metaphorical, from another field, or the question asks about composition, examples, or users instead of function.

Transfer rule: If a prompt uses figurative or niche phrasing, then translate it into the underlying real-world process before mapping choices.
Error pattern: Success came from semantic reframing: turning odd wording into a familiar mechanism and selecting the consequence that naturally follows.
Diagnostic check: Replace each unusual phrase with a plain-language equivalent, ask “what physically happens here?”, then eliminate any option lacking a causal link.
Use when: Relevant for riddling multiple-choice items, metaphor-heavy wording, puns, or descriptions of bodily, physical, or everyday processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question depends on memorized facts, formal definitions, or explicit calculations rather than interpretation.

Transfer rule: If a question describes raw materials being pulped, liquefied, or dried, then map it to products made from processed fiber sheets, not intact wood items.
Error pattern: Successful cue-matching from manufacturing steps to the product category rather than surface associations with the source material.
Diagnostic check: List which options require preserving solid wood shape versus converting wood into slurry or fibers; choose only an option consistent with slurry-to-sheet processing.
Use when: The prompt includes production verbs, material transformations, or factory steps that distinguish processed-fiber goods from carved or assembled wood goods.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are all pulped-fiber products or when the process description is metaphorical, incomplete, or unrelated to manufacturing.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how an arid-adapted organism responds to brief seasonal rain, then choose the function that conserves the resource for later dry periods.
Error pattern: Success came from applying habitat adaptation reasoning instead of reacting to humorous or anthropomorphic distractors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, name the habitat constraint, the temporary resource pulse, and the survival mechanism; confirm they fit as one coherent adaptation chain.
Use when: Relevant for biology items about plants or animals in deserts, drought-prone regions, or other environments with scarce but episodic resources.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is about immediate behavioral reactions, human-managed systems, or species not shaped by resource scarcity.

Transfer rule: If choices include one practical preparation tool and others are irrelevant or harmful, then pick the tool required for cooking.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the task’s real-world necessity and rejecting distractors by basic commonsense function.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this directly help make the food ready to eat in ordinary cooking?” Eliminate anything decorative, unrelated, or dangerous.
Use when: The question asks what is needed to prepare, use, or complete an everyday activity and options mix plausible tools with absurd distractors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is metaphorical, fictional, safety-prohibited, or depends on a special setting where ordinary preparation assumptions fail.

Transfer rule: If asked which object has a material-specific resonating body, then match the sound-producing structure to the instrument family and its usual construction.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by how sound is produced and what part serves as the resonator, not by surface familiarity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, name the vibrating source and the resonating body; choose only one whose resonator is typically wooden.
Use when: This fits instrument-identification questions involving materials, resonance, or families such as strings, winds, and struck objects.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are unusual modern variants, composite materials, or the question asks about pitch mechanism instead of resonator material.

Transfer rule: If a dissolved substance alters a liquid’s phase behavior, then check for freezing-point depression before choosing unrelated properties.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a standard colligative-property effect instead of being distracted by irrelevant physical quantities.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does adding a solute mainly change phase-change temperatures while leaving light, magnetism, and total energy nonbasic here?”
Use when: Apply this to questions about mixing a solute into a solvent and asking which bulk property decreases.
Boundary: Ignore when the substance reacts chemically, concentration effects are extreme, or the question targets optical, magnetic, or energy transfer mechanisms.

Transfer rule: If an animal trait is highlighted, then infer its most likely survival function in feeding, defense, or reproduction before considering human-centered choices.
Error pattern: Success came from using ecological purpose rather than literal or anthropomorphic distractors.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Who directly benefits the animal’s survival from this trait right now?”; reject options centered on humans, observers, or helping enemies.
Use when: The question asks why an organism has a body feature, signal, color, sound, or behavior in a basic biology context.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt specifies artificial training, human intervention, fictional worlds, or unusual experimental conditions.

Transfer rule: If asked what a magnet would stick to, then choose the option typically made of iron or steel, not wood, plastic, or food.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each option by material and applying magnetism only to ferromagnetic materials.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, label its usual material; ask “Would a common magnet attract this material in everyday use?” and pick only those marked yes.
Use when: This applies to basic science questions about magnetic attraction among everyday objects with different materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the item could be nonmagnetic metal, alloy-dependent, coated, tiny, or the question asks about electrical effects instead.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which activity belongs to a biological or organic life cycle, then choose the option involving reproduction or living processes.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the domain correctly and rejecting dramatic physical or cosmic events as category mismatches.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can this occur as a normal process of living organisms?” Eliminate anything in astrophysics, disasters, or inanimate phenomena.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-choice items contrasting life-process terms with unrelated scientific or catastrophic events.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is metaphorical, mythic, symbolic, or about nonliteral “wheels” or “life” frameworks.

Transfer rule: If an action changes an object by compressing it into a denser, irregular shape, then choose the term for compression rather than bending flat or returning to a prior state.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the verb to the dominant physical transformation, not to a smaller sub-action.
Diagnostic check: Name the start shape and end shape; ask whether the main change is compression, crease-making, making level, or undoing.
Use when: Apply this on basic vocabulary items about physical transformations of familiar materials or objects.
